def update_values(
    self,
    registry: VariableRegistry,
    current_time: datetime,
    time_step: timedelta,

):
    """ Updates values in the LHS matrix based on the timestep. 

    A sparse matrix is a matrix that is mostly zeroes. Here, we will set up an NCELL x NCELL sparse matrix. 
        - The diagonal values represent the reference cell ("P")
        - The non-zero off-diagonal values represent the other cells that share an edge with that cell:
            i.e., neighboring cell ("N") that shares a face ("f") with P. 

    This function populates the sparse matrix with:
        - Values on the Diagonal (associated with the cell with the same index as that row/column):
            - Load at the t+1 timestep (volume at the t + 1 timestep / change in time)
            - Sum of diffusion coefficients associated with a cell      
            - FOR DRY CELLS ONLY (volume = 0), insert a dummy value (1) so that the matrix is not singular
        - Values Off-Diagonal:
            - Coefficient to the diffusion term at the t+1 timestep 
        - Advection: a special case (updwinds scheme)
            - When the advection coefficient is positive, the concentration across the face will be the reference cell ("P")
                so the coefficient will go in the diagonal. This value will then be subtracted from the corresponding neighbor cell.
            - When the advection coefficient is negative, the concentration across the face will be the neighbor cell ("N")
                so the coefficient will be off-diagonal. This value will the subtracted from the corresponding reference cell.

    Attributes:
        rows / columns: point to the row and column of each cell
        coefficients: value in the specified row, column pair in the matrix 
    """
    # get requried variables from registry
    flow_across_face = registry.get_at_time(
        FLOW_ACROSS_FACE,
        current_time
    )
    volume = registry.get_at_time(
        VOLUME,
        current_time + time_step  # use volume at t+1 timestep
    ) 
    coefficient_to_diffusion_term = registry.get_at_time(
        COEFFICIENT_TO_DIFFUSION_TERM,
        current_time
    )

    # topology information
    faces = registry.get(VOLUME)[FACES]
    edges_face1 = registry.get(EDGE_FACE_CONNECTIVITY).T[0]
    edges_face2 = registry.get(EDGE_FACE_CONNECTIVITY).T[1]

    if self.has_gate_flow:
        gate_flow = registry.get(
            GATE_FLOW,
            current_time
        )
        flow_out_gate_indices = np.where(gate_flow > 0)
        flow_in_gate_indices = np.where(gate_flow < 0)
    else:
        flow_out_gate_indices = np.array([])
        flow_in_gate_indices = np.array([])            

    # define edges where flow is flowing in versus out at current timestep
    flow_out_indices = np.where(flow_across_face > 0)[0]
    flow_out_indices_internal = np.where(
        (flow_across_face > 0) & \
        (np.isin(flow_across_face.nedge, self.internal_edges))
    )[0]
    flow_in_indices = np.where(
        (flow_across_face < 0) & \
        (np.isin(flow_across_face.nedge, self.internal_edges))
    )

    # find empty cells at next timestep
    empty_cells = np.where(
        (volume.values == 0) & \
        (np.isin(volume.nface, np.arange(self.real_cell_count)))
    )[0]

    # initialize arrays that will define the sparse matrix 
    self.start_index = 0
    self.end_index = 0
    self.__init_matrix_values(
        flow_out_indices,
        flow_in_indices,
        empty_cells,
        flow_out_gate_indices,
        flow_in_gate_indices,
    )

    # fill in matrix values
    self.__fill_empty_cells(empty_cells)
    self.__fill_load_values(volume, faces, registry.get(CHANGE_IN_TIME))
    self.__fill_diffusion_values(
        coefficient_to_diffusion_term,
        edges_face1,
        edges_face2,
    )
    self.__fill_advection_values(
        flow_across_face,
        edges_face1,
        edges_face2,
        flow_out_indices,
        flow_out_indices_internal,
        flow_in_indices,
    )
    if self.has_gate_flow:
        self.__fill_advection_values(
            flow_across_face,
            registry.get(GATE_CONNECTIVITY).T[0],
            registry.get(GATE_CONNECTIVITY).T[1],
            flow_out_gate_indices,
            flow_out_gate_indices,
            flow_in_gate_indices,
        )

class RHS:
    def __init__(
        self,
        registry: VariableRegistry,
    ):
        """
        Initialize the right-hand side matrix of concentrations based on user-defined boundary conditions. 
        """
        self.real_cell_index = registry.get(NUMBER_OF_REAL_CELLS) - 1
        self.real_cell_count = registry.get(NUMBER_OF_REAL_CELLS)
        edges_face2 = registry.get(EDGE_FACE_CONNECTIVITY).T[1]

        self.values = np.zeros(self.real_cell_count)
        self.ghost_cells = np.where(edges_face2 > self.real_cell_index)[0]

    def update_values(
        self,
        # solution: np.array,
        registry: VariableRegistry,
        current_time: datetime,
        time_step: timedelta,
        constituent_name: str,
    ):
        """ 
        Update right hand side data based on the solution from the previous timestep
            solution: solution from solving the sparse matrix 
        """
        constituent_data = registry.get_at_time(
            constituent_name,
            current_time
        )

        self.concentrations = constituent_data.fillna(0.0)[0:self.real_cell_count]
        # solver.values[0:]

        # solver = np.zeros(
        #     len(
        #         mesh[name].isel(time=t)
        #     )
        # ) 
        # solver[0:self.nreal_count] = solution
        # solver[self.input_array[t].nonzero()] = self.input_array[t][self.input_array[t].nonzero()] 
        self.values[:] = self.__calculate_rhs(registry, current_time, time_step, constituent_name)

    def _calculate_load(self, registry: VariableRegistry, current_time: datetime):
        """Calculate the load 
        Returns:
            load (xr.DataArray):            (M/T) Calculated as volume (L3) * concentration (M/L3) / time (T).
        """
        volume = registry.get_at_time(
            VOLUME,
            current_time
        )[0:self.real_cell_count]
        delta_time = registry.get(CHANGE_IN_TIME)
        load = volume * self.concentrations / delta_time
        return load

    def _calculate_ghost_cell_values(
            self,
            registry: VariableRegistry,
            current_time: datetime,
            time_step: timedelta,
            constituent_name: str,
        ):
        """
        Determine the ghost cells that are flowing into the model mesh
            and the ghost cells that are receiving flow out of the model mesh.

        Args:
            mesh (xr.Dataset):              UGRID-complaint xarray Dataset with all data required for the transport equation.
            t (int):                        Timestep

        Returns:
            ghost_cells_in (np.ndarray):    Indices of ghost cells that are flowing in to the model mesh
            ghost_cells_out (np.ndarray):   Indices of ghost cells that are receiving flow out of the model mesh.
        """
        ghost_cells_in = np.zeros(self.real_cell_count)
        ghost_cells_out = np.zeros(self.real_cell_count)
        ghost_cells_in[:] = self._ghost_cell(
            registry,
            current_time,
            time_step,
            constituent_name,
            flowing_in=True
        )[0:self.real_cell_count]
        ghost_cells_out[:] = self._ghost_cell(
            registry=registry,
            current_time=current_time,
            time_step=time_step,
            constituent_name=constituent_name,
            flowing_in=False
        )[0:self.real_cell_count]

        return ghost_cells_in, ghost_cells_out

    def __calculate_rhs(
            self,
            registry: VariableRegistry,
            current_time: datetime,
            time_step: timedelta,
            constituent_name: str,
        ):
        """
        Calculates the Right Hand Side matrix,
            including the load at the current timestep for internal (real) cells,
            and known transport terms associated with connected external (ghost) cells.
        """
        load = self._calculate_load(registry, current_time)
        ghost_cells_in, ghost_cells_out = self._calculate_ghost_cell_values(registry, current_time, time_step, constituent_name)
        return load + ghost_cells_in + ghost_cells_out


    def _transport_mechanisms(self, flowing_in: bool):
        """
        Determines which transport mechanisms associated with ghost cells should
            be included in the right hand side of the matrix. This function also 
            determines a condition to help identify ghost cells that are flowing in/
            out of the mesh, based on the sign of the edge velocity. 
            1. Ghost cells flowing in to the model mesh will include both advection
            and diffusion terms under the upwind differencing scheme. Ghost cells flowing
            into the model mesh will have an edge velocity that is less than zero in RAS. 
            2. Ghost cells receiving flow from the model mesh will only include
            diffusion terms; the advection term for these cells will be on the left 
            hand side of the equation under the upwind differencing scheme. These cells
            will have an edge velocity that is greater than zero in RAS.

        Args:
            flowing_in (bool):              Indicator of whether the function should return values
                                                for ghost cells flowing in to the model (True) or
                                                receiving flow out of the model (false).
        Returns:
            advection (bool):               True if advection terms should be included on the RHS, otherwise False.
            diffusion (bool):               True if diffusion terms should be included on the RHS, otherwise False.
            condition (np.ufunc):           np.less for ghost cells flowing into the model,
                                                np.greater for ghost cells receiving flow out of the model. 
        """
        diffusion = True
        if flowing_in:
            advection = True
            condition = np.less
        else:
            advection = False
            condition = np.greater
        return advection, diffusion, condition

    def _define_arrays(self, registry: VariableRegistry, advection: bool):
        """Initialize arrays for advection and diffusion terms associated with ghost cells.

        Returns:
            advection_edge(np.ndarray):     Empty numpy array with a length equal to the number of edges in the model.
            advection_face(np.ndarray):     Empty numpy array with a length equal to the number of faces in the model.
            diffusion_edge(np.ndarray):     Empty numpy array with a length equal to the number of edges in the model.
            diffusion_face(np.ndarray):     Empty numpy array with a length equal to the number of faces in the model.
        """
        advection_edge = None
        advection_face = None
        diffusion_edge = None
        diffusion_face = None

        nface = registry.get(NFACE)
        nedge = registry.get(NEDGE) 

        if advection:
            advection_edge = np.zeros(nedge)
            advection_face = np.zeros(nface)
        diffusion_edge = np.zeros(nedge)
        diffusion_face = np.zeros(nface)
        return advection_edge, advection_face, diffusion_edge, diffusion_face

    def _edge_to_face(
            self,
            edge_array: np.array,
            face_array: np.array,
            mesh_array: xr.DataArray,
            index_list: list,
            internal_cell_index
        ):
        """Transfer values associated with edges to corresponding internal face.
````
        Args:
            edge_array (np.ndarray):        Numpy array with a length equal to the number of edges in the model.
                                                Populated with edge values between a ghost cell and and an internal cell. 
            face_array (np.ndarray):        Empty numpy array with a length equal to the number of faces in the model.
            mesh_array (xr.DataArray):      Values associated with an edge for a model mesh.
            index_list (list):              List of ghost cells meeting flowing in or out condition
            internal_cell_index:            Internal cell for a ghost cell edge.

        Returns:
            face_array (np.ndarray):         Numpy array with a length equal to the number of faces in the model.
                                                Populated with values previously associated with edges between a ghost and internal cell,
                                                now the values falls on the indices associated with the internal cell. 
        """    
        edge_array[index_list] = abs(mesh_array[index_list])
        values = np.where(edge_array != 0)[0]
        face_array[np.array(internal_cell_index)] = edge_array[values]
        return face_array

    def _ghost_cell(
            self,
            registry: VariableRegistry,
            current_time: datetime,
            time_step: timedelta,
            constituent_name: str,
            flowing_in: bool
        ):
        """
        Manages terms on the right hand side of the matrix associated with ghost cells
            that are flowing in or out of the model mesh.
        Returns:
            add_to_rhs (np.ndarray):        Array of transport terms associated with ghost cells
                                                that should be added to the right hand side.
        """
        advection, diffusion, condition = self._transport_mechanisms(flowing_in)
        advection_edge, advection_face, diffusion_edge, diffusion_face = self._define_arrays(registry, advection)

        edge_velocity = registry.get_at_time(
            EDGE_VELOCITY,
            current_time,
        )
        edges_face1 = registry.get(EDGE_FACE_CONNECTIVITY).T[0]
        edges_face2 = registry.get(EDGE_FACE_CONNECTIVITY).T[1]

        velocity_indices = np.where(condition(edge_velocity, 0))[0]
        advection_coefficient = registry.get_at_time(FLOW_ACROSS_FACE, current_time)
        diffusion_coefficient = registry.get_at_time(DIFFUSION_COEFFICIENT, current_time)
        diffusion_term = registry.get_at_time(COEFFICIENT_TO_DIFFUSION_TERM, current_time)
        index_list = np.intersect1d(velocity_indices, self.ghost_cells)
        internal_cell_index = edges_face1[index_list]
        external_cell_index = edges_face2[index_list]

        concentration_multipliers = np.zeros(registry.get(NFACE))
        concentration_multipliers[internal_cell_index] = registry.get_at_time(
            constituent_name,
            current_time + time_step
        )[external_cell_index]

        if len(index_list) != 0:
            if advection:
                advection_face[:] = self._edge_to_face(
                    advection_edge,
                    advection_face,
                    advection_coefficient,
                    index_list,
                    internal_cell_index
                    )
            if diffusion and diffusion_coefficient !=0:
                diffusion_face[:] = self._edge_to_face(
                    diffusion_edge,
                    diffusion_face,
                    diffusion_term,
                    index_list,
                    internal_cell_index
                    )

        if flowing_in:
            add_to_rhs = advection_face + diffusion_face
        else:
            add_to_rhs = diffusion_face

        add_to_rhs = add_to_rhs * concentration_multipliers

        return add_to_rhs

def __calculate_rhs(
        self,
        registry: VariableRegistry,
        current_time: datetime,
        time_step: timedelta,
        constituent_name: str,
    ):
    """
    Calculates the Right Hand Side matrix,
        including the load at the current timestep for internal (real) cells,
        and known transport terms associated with connected external (ghost) cells.
    """
    load = self._calculate_load(registry, current_time)
    ghost_cells_in, ghost_cells_out = self._calculate_ghost_cell_values(registry, current_time, time_step, constituent_name)
    return load + ghost_cells_in + ghost_cells_out

def calculate_distances_cell_centroids(
        registry: VariableRegistry,
    ) -> np.array:
    """ Calculate the distance between cell centroids

    Args:
        registry: VariableRegistry 

    Returns:
        dist_data (np.array):   Array of distances between all cell centroids 
    """
    # Get northings and eastings of relevant faces 
    face_x = registry.get(FACE_X)
    face_y = registry.get(FACE_Y)
    edges_face1 = registry.get(EDGE_FACE_CONNECTIVITY).T[0]
    edges_face2 = registry.get(EDGE_FACE_CONNECTIVITY).T[1]

    x1_coords = face_x[edges_face1]  #mesh['face_x'][mesh['edges_face1']]
    y1_coords = face_y[edges_face1]
    x2_coords = face_x[edges_face2] 
    y2_coords = face_y[edges_face2]

    # calculate distance 
    dist_data = xr.DataArray(
        np.sqrt((x1_coords - x2_coords)**2 + (y1_coords - y2_coords)**2),
        dims = ('nedge'),  ## TODO: add unit management
    )
    return DataArrayVariable(dist_data)

def calculate_coeff_to_diffusion_term(
        registry: VariableRegistry,
    ) -> np.array:
    """ Calculate the coefficient to the diffusion term. 

    For each edge, this is calculated as:
    (Edge vertical area * diffusion coefficient) / (distance between cells) 

    Args:
        registry: VariableRegistry

    Returns:
        diffusion_array (np.array):     Array of diffusion coefficients associated with each edge

    """
    edge_vertical_area = registry.get(EDGE_VERTICAL_AREA)
    face_to_face_distance = registry.get(FACE_TO_FACE_DISTANCE)
    diffusion_coefficient = registry.get(DIFFUSION_COEFFICIENT)

    diffusion_array = edge_vertical_area * diffusion_coefficient / face_to_face_distance
    return DataArrayVariable(diffusion_array)

def calculate_wetted_surface_area(
    registry: VariableRegistry
):
    """
    Calculate wetted surface area based on elevation-volume lookup table.
    """
    # Define required dimensions for lookup xarray
    nface = len(registry.get(FACE_SURFACE_AREA)[FACES])
    ntime = len(registry.get(VOLUME)["time"])
    lookup_volumes = registry.get(LOOKUP_VOLUME)
    lookup_areas = registry.get(LOOKUP_WETTED_SURFACE_AREA)

    # fill null lookup values with the maximum
    # this will help the interpolation function work correctly for large values
    lookup_volumes = lookup_volumes.fillna(lookup_volumes.max(dim='index', skipna=True))
    lookup_areas = lookup_areas.fillna(lookup_areas.max(dim='index', skipna=True))

    # preallocate output array
    result = xr.DataArray(
        np.full((ntime, nface), np.nan),
        dims=[TIME, FACES],
        coords={
            TIME: registry.get(VOLUME)["time"],
            FACES:np.arange(nface),
        }
    )

    # loop through real faces, get wetted surface area for all timesteps
    for nf in lookup_areas.nface:
        volumes = registry.get(VOLUME).sel(nface=nf).values
        result[:,  nf] = np.interp(
            volumes,
            lookup_volumes.sel(nface=nf).values,
            lookup_areas.sel(nface=nf).values,
            left=lookup_areas.sel(nface=nf).values[0],  # interp to lowermost value
            right=lookup_areas.sel(nface=nf).values[-1],  # interp to largest value
        )

    # Convert result back to xarray.DataArray
    return DataArrayVariable(result)

def calculate_average_depth(
    registry: VariableRegistry   
):
    """Calculate average depth based on volume and wetted surface area."""
    # If wetted surface area does not exist, calculate it.
    if WETTED_SURFACE_AREA not in registry:
        wetted_surface_area = calculate_wetted_surface_area(registry)
        registry.register(
            WETTED_SURFACE_AREA,
            wetted_surface_area,
        )

    # Calculate average depth
    average_depth = xr.where(
        registry.get(WETTED_SURFACE_AREA) > 0,
        registry.get(VOLUME) / registry.get(WETTED_SURFACE_AREA),
        0
    )

    return DataArrayVariable(average_depth)

def calculate_maximum_depth(
    registry: VariableRegistry
):
    """Calculate the maximum depth based on water surface elevation."""
    minimum_elevation = registry.get(LOOKUP_ELEVATION)
    # volume elevation lookup only has real cells: expand dimensions to include all cells
    minimum_elevation = minimum_elevation.reindex(nface=np.arange(len(registry.get(FACE_X))))
    maxiumum_depth = registry.get(WATER_SURFACE_ELEVATION) - minimum_elevation

    return DataArrayVariable(maxiumum_depth)

docs.title: Developer Guide
docs.text:
This section provides guidance for contributors working on the ClearWater framework. It covers the architecture, how to add new water quality processes, testing conventions, and the contribution workflow.

ClearWater organizes the numerical kernels around an explicit Process abstract base class, a shared VariableRegistry for state, and chunked-zarr storage for memory-efficient long simulations. The pages below walk new contributors through this architecture and the recipes that keep new code consistent with the rest of the framework.

docs.title: In this section
docs.text:
• Architecture Walkthrough describes the three-package layout (ClearWater-Riverine, ClearWater-Modules, ClearWater-Data), the Process lifecycle, the VariableRegistry, the Model orchestrator, YAML-driven assembly, and the chunked versus full simulation modes.
  • Adding a New Process provides a step-by-step recipe for implementing a new water quality process as a Process subclass, including registration, coupling with other processes, temperature correction, and parity tests against the published Fortran reference.
  • Testing Strategy describes the project's testing layers: unit tests, reference-parity tests, integration tests, how to run them locally, and what continuous integration (CI) expects on every pull request.
  • Contributing Guidelines documents the forking workflow, branch naming, commit message conventions, code style, and the pull request checklist.

New to the codebase?

Read the Architecture Walkthrough first, then skim Adding a New Process to see how the architecture is used in practice. Both pages reference the reference implementations in src/clearwater_modules/processes/.

docs.title: Adding a New Process
docs.text:
This page describes the end-to-end recipe for adding a new water quality process to ClearWater. It assumes you have read the Architecture Walkthrough and understand the Process lifecycle, the VariableRegistry, and the Model orchestrator.

The recipe has five steps:

  1. Create a Process subclass in src/clearwater_modules/processes/<name>.py.
  2. Register the class with ProcessFactory via from_config.
  3. Implement per-term rate helper methods (one per source or sink) and compose them in run.
  4. Add the new class to the RUN_ORDER list in src/clearwater_modules/processes/__init__.py.
  5. Add a reference-parity test (when a published reference exists) under tests/parity/.

This page works through a complete, compilable example: a simple first-order decay tracer. Real Nutrient Simulation Module 1 (NSM1) derivatives are more complex, but the structure is identical. Use the example as a starting template and refer to temperature.py, floating_algae.py, and nitrogen.py for richer patterns.

docs.title: Step 1. Create the Process Subclass
docs.text:
Create src/clearwater_modules/processes/tracer.py with the following skeleton.

"""First-order decay tracer process."""

from datetime import datetime, timedelta
from typing import TYPE_CHECKING

import numpy as np
import xarray as xr

from clearwater_data.custom_types import ArrayLike
from clearwater_data.variables import VariableRegistry

from clearwater_modules.processes.base import Process, ProcessFactory
from clearwater_modules.utils.conversions import arrhenius_correction

if TYPE_CHECKING:
    from clearwater_modules.model import Model


class Tracer(Process):
    """First-order decay tracer with temperature-corrected rate.

    The process integrates a single state variable, ``tracer``, with a
    first-order loss term whose rate is Arrhenius-corrected from a
    reference temperature of 20 degrees Celsius.

    Parameters
    ----------
    time_step : timedelta
        Process time step.
    decay_rate_20 : float
        First-order decay rate at 20 degrees Celsius, in day-1.
    decay_theta : float
        Arrhenius temperature correction factor (dimensionless).
    """

    variables = [
        "tracer",
        "water_temperature",
    ]

    def __init__(
        self,
        time_step: timedelta = timedelta(minutes=5),
        decay_rate_20: float = 0.1,
        decay_theta: float = 1.047,
    ) -> None:
        self.decay_rate_20 = decay_rate_20
        self.decay_theta = decay_theta
        Process.__init__(self, time_step)

The variables class attribute lists every registry key the process reads or writes. The Model uses this list to validate the registry before the simulation starts. The __init__ method stores kinetic parameters as instance attributes and calls Process.__init__ with the time_step.

Accept ArrayLike rather than float

When a parameter may vary in space (for example, a settling velocity that differs per-cell), declare it as ArrayLike rather than float. Scalars and xarray DataArray objects both satisfy the type, and downstream arithmetic broadcasts naturally.

docs.title: Step 2. Register with ProcessFactory
docs.text:
Add a from_config classmethod decorated with ProcessFactory.register directly after __init__.

    @ProcessFactory.register("tracer")
    @staticmethod
    def from_config(
        config: dict, variable_registry: VariableRegistry
    ) -> "Tracer":
        return Tracer(**config)

The short name passed to register is the identifier used in the YAML configuration. After registration, a YAML block like the following will construct the process:

processes:
  - name: tracer
    config:
      decay_rate_20: 0.2
      decay_theta: 1.05
      time_step: 300

docs.title: Step 3. Implement init_process
docs.text:
Use init_process to inspect the model for optional coupling partners. For the decay tracer the hook is minimal, but it illustrates the pattern for richer processes.

    def init_process(self, model: "Model", registry: VariableRegistry) -> None:
        """Detect optional coupling partners before the time loop starts."""
        self.use_temperature_correction = model.has_process("Temperature")

For processes that couple to others (for example, the nitrogen process reading the floating algae respiration rate), init_process is where you resolve the sibling process handle:

if model.has_process("FloatingAlgae"):
    self.floating_algae = model.get_process("FloatingAlgae")

docs.title: Step 4. Implement Per-Term Rate Methods
docs.text:
Break the derivative into one public method per source or sink term. This pattern, used by FloatingAlgae and Nitrogen, lets other processes pull individual terms as coupling inputs without recomputing the full derivative.

    def rate_decay(
        self,
        tracer: ArrayLike,
        water_temperature: ArrayLike,
    ) -> ArrayLike:
        """Compute the first-order decay rate.

        Parameters
        ----------
        tracer : ArrayLike
            Tracer concentration in mg L-1.
        water_temperature : ArrayLike
            Water temperature in degrees Celsius.

        Returns
        -------
        ArrayLike
            Decay rate in mg L-1 day-1.
        """
        k = arrhenius_correction(
            water_temperature,
            self.decay_rate_20,
            self.decay_theta,
        )
        return k * tracer

The arrhenius_correction helper in clearwater_modules/utils/conversions.py centralizes the rc20 * theta^(TwaterC - 20) pattern used across the framework. Always prefer the helper over inlining the formula so that future changes (for example, adding input validation on theta) apply everywhere.

docs.title: Step 5. Implement the run Method
docs.text:
The run method pulls inputs from the registry, composes the rate terms, integrates forward one step, clips negative concentrations, and writes the result back.

    def run(self, time: datetime, registry: VariableRegistry) -> None:
        """Advance the tracer one time step."""
        tracer = registry.get_at_time("tracer", time)
        water_temperature = registry.get_at_time("water_temperature", time)

        loss = self.rate_decay(tracer, water_temperature)

        # Explicit Euler step. Rate is in day-1; convert dt to days.
        dt_days = self.time_step.total_seconds() / 86400.0
        new_tracer = tracer - loss * dt_days

        # Clip negative concentrations that can arise from a large dt.
        new_tracer = xr.where(new_tracer < 0, 0, new_tracer)

        # Persist the updated state. THIS IS REQUIRED.
        registry.set_at_time("tracer", new_tracer, time)

Persist every state variable you update

The single most common mistake when implementing a new process is computing an updated value and failing to call registry.set_at_time. The update is silently dropped, and downstream processes see stale state. Every run method must end with a set_at_time call for every variable it updates.

Do not test for NaN with equality

xr.where(x == np.nan, 0, x) is always False under IEEE 754. Use xr.where(x.isnull(), 0, x) or xr.where(np.isnan(x), 0, x) to substitute a fallback value for missing data.

docs.title: Step 6. Register the Process in RUN_ORDER
docs.text:
Open src/clearwater_modules/processes/__init__.py and add the new class to the RUN_ORDER list. Order matters: processes that consume outputs of another process must appear after their dependency.

from clearwater_modules.processes.riverine import Riverine
from clearwater_modules.processes.temperature import Temperature
from clearwater_modules.processes.benthic_algae import BenthicAlgae
from clearwater_modules.processes.floating_algae import FloatingAlgae
from clearwater_modules.processes.nitrogen import Nitrogen
from clearwater_modules.processes.tracer import Tracer

RUN_ORDER = [
    Riverine,
    Temperature,
    BenthicAlgae,
    FloatingAlgae,
    Nitrogen,
    Tracer,
]

docs.title: Step 7. Add a Reference-Parity Test
docs.text:
For any process that has a published reference (for example, an NSM1 process from Zhang and Johnson, 2016), add a parity test that runs identical inputs through the reference and the new Process subclass and asserts the outputs agree within a documented tolerance. Use tests/parity/test_tsm_parity.py as a template.

# tests/parity/test_tracer_parity.py
from datetime import datetime, timedelta

import numpy as np
import pytest
import xarray as xr

from clearwater_modules.processes.tracer import Tracer
from .reference import tracer_reference_derivative


@pytest.fixture
def inputs():
    return {
        "tracer": xr.DataArray(np.array([1.0, 0.5, 2.0])),
        "water_temperature": xr.DataArray(np.array([15.0, 20.0, 25.0])),
    }


def test_tracer_reference_parity(inputs):
    """Tracer matches the published first-order decay reference."""
    process = Tracer(
        time_step=timedelta(minutes=5),
        decay_rate_20=0.1,
        decay_theta=1.047,
    )
    rate = process.rate_decay(
        inputs["tracer"], inputs["water_temperature"]
    )
    reference_rate = tracer_reference_derivative(
        inputs["tracer"].values,
        inputs["water_temperature"].values,
        decay_rate_20=0.1,
        decay_theta=1.047,
    )
    np.testing.assert_allclose(rate.values, reference_rate, rtol=1e-6)

Add unit tests that cover each rate_* method in isolation as well. See the Testing Strategy page for the full test taxonomy.

docs.title: Complete Example
docs.text:
The full tracer.py file, assembled from the snippets above, is a runnable starting template for new processes:

"""First-order decay tracer process."""

from datetime import datetime, timedelta
from typing import TYPE_CHECKING

import numpy as np
import xarray as xr

from clearwater_data.custom_types import ArrayLike
from clearwater_data.variables import VariableRegistry

from clearwater_modules.processes.base import Process, ProcessFactory
from clearwater_modules.utils.conversions import arrhenius_correction

if TYPE_CHECKING:
    from clearwater_modules.model import Model


class Tracer(Process):
    """First-order decay tracer with temperature-corrected rate."""

    variables = ["tracer", "water_temperature"]

    def __init__(
        self,
        time_step: timedelta = timedelta(minutes=5),
        decay_rate_20: float = 0.1,
        decay_theta: float = 1.047,
    ) -> None:
        self.decay_rate_20 = decay_rate_20
        self.decay_theta = decay_theta
        Process.__init__(self, time_step)

    @ProcessFactory.register("tracer")
    @staticmethod
    def from_config(
        config: dict, variable_registry: VariableRegistry
    ) -> "Tracer":
        return Tracer(**config)

    def init_process(self, model: "Model", registry: VariableRegistry) -> None:
        self.use_temperature_correction = model.has_process("Temperature")

    def rate_decay(
        self,
        tracer: ArrayLike,
        water_temperature: ArrayLike,
    ) -> ArrayLike:
        """Compute the first-order decay rate in mg L-1 day-1."""
        k = arrhenius_correction(
            water_temperature,
            self.decay_rate_20,
            self.decay_theta,
        )
        return k * tracer

    def run(self, time: datetime, registry: VariableRegistry) -> None:
        tracer = registry.get_at_time("tracer", time)
        water_temperature = registry.get_at_time("water_temperature", time)

        loss = self.rate_decay(tracer, water_temperature)

        dt_days = self.time_step.total_seconds() / 86400.0
        new_tracer = tracer - loss * dt_days
        new_tracer = xr.where(new_tracer < 0, 0, new_tracer)

        registry.set_at_time("tracer", new_tracer, time)

docs.title: Checklist Before Opening a Pull Request
docs.text:
• [ ] Process subclass lives in src/clearwater_modules/processes/<name>.py.
  • [ ] variables class attribute lists every registry key read or written.
  • [ ] __init__ accepts all kinetic parameters with sensible defaults and calls Process.__init__ with the time_step.
  • [ ] from_config is decorated with @ProcessFactory.register("<name>").
  • [ ] init_process resolves optional couplings via model.has_process and model.get_process.
  • [ ] Each source and sink term has its own public rate_* method with a NumPy-style docstring.
  • [ ] run calls registry.set_at_time for every state variable it updates.
  • [ ] Temperature-dependent rates use arrhenius_correction from clearwater_modules/utils/conversions.py.
  • [ ] The process is added to RUN_ORDER in process dependency order.
  • [ ] Unit tests cover each rate_* method and the integration step in run.
  • [ ] A reference-parity test (where applicable) asserts the implementation matches the published reference within a documented tolerance.

See the Contributing Guidelines for the pull request workflow and Testing Strategy for the full test taxonomy.

docs.title: Architecture Walkthrough
docs.text: This page describes the ClearWater architecture. Each kinetic module is implemented as an explicit Process abstract base class (ABC) subclass, processes share state through a VariableRegistry, and long simulations stream through a chunked-zarr backend. New contributors should read this page before adding code to clearwater_modules/.

docs.title: Three-Package Layout
docs.text:
ClearWater is distributed as three cooperating Python packages. Each package owns a distinct concern, and the dependency arrows flow in one direction only.

Package Responsibility Depends on ClearWater-Data Variable registry, data sources, chunked zarr storage, array type aliases None within the project ClearWater-Modules Water quality kinetics; the Process ABC, Model orchestrator, and individual processes (temperature, algae, nitrogen, etc.) ClearWater-Data ClearWater-Riverine 2D hydraulic transport on unstructured meshes; couples hydraulics to the water quality modules ClearWater-Data, ClearWater-Modules

ClearWater-Data defines the shared primitives (VariableRegistry, DataSource, ChunkedDataSource, ChunkedZarrDataStore, the ArrayLike type alias). ClearWater-Modules builds the kinetic processes on top of those primitives. ClearWater-Riverine supplies the transport layer and orchestrates coupled hydraulic and water quality simulations.

docs.title: Overall Data Flow
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    Config[YAML config] --> Factory[ProcessFactory]
    Factory --> Model
    DataSources[DataSource and<br/>ChunkedDataSource] --> Registry[VariableRegistry]
    Model --> Registry
    Registry --> P1[Process: Temperature]
    Registry --> P2[Process: FloatingAlgae]
    Registry --> P3[Process: Nitrogen]
    P1 --> Registry
    P2 --> Registry
    P3 --> Registry
    Registry --> Output[ChunkedZarrDataStore]

The Model class reads a YAML configuration, assembles the configured processes via ProcessFactory, loads input data into the VariableRegistry, steps through time calling each Process.run(time, registry) in order, and writes the selected output variables to a zarr store.

docs.title: The Process Abstract Base Class
docs.text:
Every water quality process is a subclass of Process defined in clearwater_modules/processes/base.py. The base class specifies a three-phase lifecycle.

from abc import ABC, abstractmethod
from datetime import datetime, timedelta
from clearwater_data.variables import VariableRegistry


class Process(ABC):
    variables: list[str] = []
    time_step_seconds: int

    def __init__(self, time_step: timedelta) -> None:
        self.time_step = time_step
        self.time_step_seconds = self.time_step.total_seconds()

    @classmethod
    def from_config(cls, config: dict, variable_registry: VariableRegistry) -> "Process":
        return cls(**config)

    def init_process(self, model: "Model", registry: VariableRegistry) -> None:
        """One-time setup before the time loop begins."""
        pass

    def validate(self, registry: VariableRegistry) -> None:
        for variable in self.variables:
            if variable not in registry:
                raise ValueError(f"Variable {variable} not registered for process.")

    def finalize_process(self, model: "Model", registry: VariableRegistry) -> None:
        """Cleanup hook called after the time loop (or each chunk)."""
        return None

    @abstractmethod
    def run(self, time: datetime, registry: VariableRegistry) -> None:
        """Advance the process state one time step."""
        raise NotImplementedError

The three lifecycle hooks are:

  1. init_process(model, registry) is called once before the time loop begins. The hook inspects the model for coupling partners (for example, model.has_process("FloatingAlgae")) and sets per-process flags that control which source and sink terms are active.
  2. run(time, registry) advances the process one time step. The method pulls inputs from the registry via registry.get_at_time(var, time), computes the derivative, integrates forward, and writes the result back via registry.set_at_time(var, value, time).
  3. finalize_process(model, registry) is called after the time loop completes. In chunked mode, the Model calls finalize_process at the end of each chunk, which gives processes a hook to flush state or record diagnostics.

The variables class attribute names every registry key the process reads or writes. The validate method checks that every listed variable is present in the registry before the simulation starts.

docs.title: The VariableRegistry
docs.text:
The VariableRegistry, defined in ClearWater-Data, is the single source of truth for simulation state. Processes never pass state to one another directly. Instead, each process reads inputs from the registry and writes outputs to the registry.

The registry exposes time-indexed accessors so that processes with different time steps can read consistent snapshots:

# Read the current-time value of a variable
water_temperature = registry.get_at_time("water_temperature", time)

# Write an updated value at the current time
registry.set_at_time("water_temperature", new_water_temperature, time)

Because state lives in the registry, inter-process coupling is explicit and traceable. For example, the nitrogen process reaches the floating algae process via model.get_process("FloatingAlgae") to read the algal respiration rate, then computes the ammonium source term from that rate and writes the updated ammonium concentration back to the registry.

Always persist state

A Process.run method that computes an updated value but does not call registry.set_at_time silently drops the update. This is the most common pitfall when implementing a new process. Every run method must end with set_at_time calls for every state variable it updates.

docs.title: The Model Orchestrator
docs.text:
The Model class in clearwater_modules/model.py owns the time loop. At construction time the Model receives:

  • A tuple of Process instances, in the order they should run each step.
  • A VariableRegistry.
  • A dictionary mapping variable names to DataSource or ChunkedDataSource objects.
  • Simulation bounds (start_time, end_time, time_step).
  • The list of output variable names to persist.
  • An optional chunk_size, which switches the model into chunked mode.

The simplified time loop for a non-chunked run is:

def run(self) -> None:
    if not self.__init_complete:
        self.__init_model()
    current_time = self.__start_time
    while current_time < self.__end_time:
        current_time_seconds = current_time.timestamp()
        for process in self.__processes:
            if current_time_seconds % process.time_step_seconds == 0:
                process.run(current_time, self.__registry)
        current_time += self.__time_step
    self.__save_output_model(self.__start_time, self.__end_time)

The modulo check on time_step_seconds allows processes with different cadences to coexist. A process with a 15-minute time step advances only on time stamps that are multiples of 900 seconds; a process with a 5-minute time step advances every 300 seconds.

Two helper methods on Model support inter-process coupling:

if model.has_process("FloatingAlgae"):
    algae = model.get_process("FloatingAlgae")
    respiration = algae.rate_respiration(...)

Processes call these helpers from init_process to detect optional couplings and from run to pull source or sink terms from sibling processes.

docs.title: ProcessFactory and YAML Assembly
docs.text:
The ProcessFactory, also in base.py, is a registry of Process constructors keyed by short names. Each Process subclass registers itself by decorating its from_config classmethod:

class FloatingAlgae(Process):
    @ProcessFactory.register("floating_algae")
    @staticmethod
    def from_config(config: dict, variable_registry: VariableRegistry) -> "FloatingAlgae":
        return FloatingAlgae(**config)

The YAML configuration lists the processes to run along with their kinetic parameters:

processes:
  - name: temperature
    config:
      wind_a: 0.3
      wind_b: 1.5
      wind_c: 1.0
      time_step: 300
  - name: floating_algae
    config:
      growth_rate_max: 2.5
      settling_velocity: 0.15
      time_step: 300

At startup, the configuration loader calls ProcessFactory.from_config(name, config, registry) for each entry, which returns the constructed Process instance. The assembled tuple of processes is then passed to the Model along with the registry, data sources, and output settings.

docs.title: Chunked Versus Full Simulation Modes
docs.text:
The Model supports two execution modes:

  • Full mode holds the entire simulation history in memory. The registry is populated once from all data sources, the time loop advances, and the output is written at the end.
  • Chunked mode streams through the simulation in time-chunked windows. On each chunk boundary the Model reads the next chunk from any ChunkedDataSource objects, runs the inner time loop over the chunk, writes the chunk's output to the ChunkedZarrDataStore, and calls finalize_process on each Process.

Chunked mode is what makes long simulations feasible on machines with limited memory. A full-year hourly simulation on a fine mesh does not fit in random-access memory (RAM); a chunked run with a one-week chunk size does.

When to choose which mode

Use full mode for short development runs and for debugging. Use chunked mode for production runs, for any simulation longer than a few days on a non-trivial mesh, and whenever output must be streamed rather than accumulated.

docs.title: Where to Look Next
docs.text:
• Adding a New Process walks through the recipe for implementing a new Process subclass end-to-end.
  • Testing Strategy describes how to validate a new process against the published Fortran reference implementation.
  • The reference implementations live in src/clearwater_modules/processes/. The temperature.py file is the most thorough example of the pattern.

docs.title: Contributing Guidelines
docs.text: The ClearWater project welcomes contributions from the scientific and engineering community. This page describes the workflow, conventions, and expectations for contributors. New contributors should read this page alongside the Architecture Walkthrough before opening a pull request.

docs.title: Development Setup
docs.text:
1. Fork the repository on GitHub into your own account.

  2. Clone your fork locally and add the upstream repository as a remote:

    git clone git@github.com:<your-username>/ClearWater-modules.git
cd ClearWater-modules
git remote add upstream https://github.com/EcohydrologyTeam/ClearWater-modules.git

  3. Create an isolated environment. The project uses pixi for environment management; conda and pip also work with the pinned versions in pyproject.toml.

    pixi install
pixi shell

  4. Verify the install by running the test suite (see Testing Strategy).

docs.title: Branching Workflow
docs.text:
The project follows a standard fork-and-pull workflow. The main branch is protected and should not receive direct pushes; all changes go through pull requests.

Create a feature branch from main for any change. Long-running development series may use a shared integration branch, in which case its name and base will be called out in the repository README.

Use descriptive branch names that include a short category prefix:

Prefix Purpose Example feature/ New functionality feature/phosphorus-process fix/ Bug fix fix/nitrogen-set-at-time docs/ Documentation only docs/process-recipe test/ Test additions or refactors test/parity-benthic-algae refactor/ Non-behavioral code changes refactor/conversions-module

docs.title: Commit Messages
docs.text:
The project uses short, imperative commit messages that describe what the commit does, not what the author did.

  • Use the imperative mood (e.g., "Add phosphorus process" rather than "Added phosphorus process").
  • Keep the subject line under 72 characters.
  • When a commit is non-trivial, include a body separated from the subject by a blank line that explains the reasoning and any behavioral consequences.
  • Reference related issues or pull requests (PRs) using #<number> in the body.

Example:

Add reference-parity test for FloatingAlgae

Runs identical inputs through the published Fortran reference and
the FloatingAlgae process and asserts per-timestep outputs match
within 1e-6 relative tolerance. Closes #142.

docs.title: Code Style
docs.text:
The project follows PEP 8 with a few project conventions.

  • Format Python code with black and sort imports with isort. Both tools are configured in pyproject.toml.
  • Annotate all public functions and class methods with type hints. Array arguments should use the ArrayLike alias exported by clearwater_data when they may be scalars or xarray objects.
  • Write NumPy-style docstrings for every public class, method, and function. Each docstring should include a one-line summary, a Parameters section, a Returns section when applicable, and a Notes or References section where relevant.
  • Use explicit variable names for state, rate coefficients, and stoichiometric ratios. Match the case used in the source code when referring to existing symbols in docstrings and comments.

Example docstring:

def rate_decay(
    self,
    concentration: ArrayLike,
    water_temperature: ArrayLike,
) -> ArrayLike:
    """Compute the first-order decay rate of the tracer.

    Parameters
    ----------
    concentration : ArrayLike
        Tracer concentration in mg L-1.
    water_temperature : ArrayLike
        Water temperature in degrees Celsius.

    Returns
    -------
    ArrayLike
        Decay rate in mg L-1 day-1.
    """

docs.title: Pull Request Expectations
docs.text:
Before opening a pull request, confirm the following.

  1. The branch is rebased on the latest target branch and has no merge conflicts.
  2. All tests pass locally (pytest tests/).
  3. New code has unit tests, and any new Process subclass has a reference-parity test (see Testing Strategy).
  4. New public API has NumPy-style docstrings.
  5. The documentation under docs/ is updated if the change affects user-facing behavior or developer workflow.

Open the pull request against the branch you forked from. Include in the description:

  • A summary of the change and its motivation.
  • A checklist of tests added or updated.
  • Any behavioral changes or breaking API changes, called out explicitly.
  • Links to related issues or design documents.

Keep pull requests focused

Unrelated refactors, formatting sweeps, and scope expansions should land in separate pull requests. Small, focused PRs are merged faster and are easier to review.

docs.title: Reporting Issues
docs.text: Use GitHub Issues to report bugs and request features. Include a minimal reproducible example, the ClearWater version, Python version, operating system, and the full error traceback.

docs.title: Testing Strategy
docs.text:
ClearWater uses pytest for all automated testing. Tests are organized into three layers that address different risks: unit tests confirm that individual rate methods are numerically correct, reference-parity tests confirm that the Python implementation reproduces the published Fortran NSM reference within a documented tolerance, and integration tests confirm that the coupled model runs end-to-end and produces plausible output.

New contributors should add tests in all three layers when they add a new Process subclass. The sections below describe what each layer is responsible for, where the tests live, and how to run them.

docs.title: Unit Tests
docs.text:
Unit tests exercise a single method of a single class with synthetic inputs. They live under tests/unit/<process>/ and are the fastest feedback loop during development.

For a new Process subclass, add a unit test for each public rate_* method. Each test should construct the process with explicit kinetic parameters, call the rate method with known inputs, and compare against a value computed by hand or from the closed-form expression.

# tests/unit/tracer/test_rate_decay.py
from datetime import timedelta

import numpy as np
import xarray as xr

from clearwater_modules.processes.tracer import Tracer


def test_rate_decay_scales_with_concentration():
    """Decay rate scales linearly with concentration at fixed temperature."""
    process = Tracer(
        time_step=timedelta(minutes=5),
        decay_rate_20=0.1,
        decay_theta=1.047,
    )
    tracer = xr.DataArray(np.array([1.0, 2.0, 4.0]))
    temperature = xr.DataArray(np.array([20.0, 20.0, 20.0]))

    rate = process.rate_decay(tracer, temperature)

    np.testing.assert_allclose(rate.values, [0.1, 0.2, 0.4])

Unit tests should not depend on a running Model and should not read files from disk. Use small, fixed-size xarray DataArray inputs that make the expected output calculable by hand.

docs.title: Reference-Parity Tests
docs.text:
Reference-parity tests guarantee that the Python implementation of an NSM1 process reproduces the published Fortran reference (Zhang and Johnson, 2016) within a documented tolerance. Each test runs identical inputs through the reference numerical solution and the corresponding Process subclass, then asserts the outputs match. These tests live under tests/parity/ with a test_*_parity.py naming convention. The tests/parity/test_tsm_parity.py file is the canonical template.

A parity test should cover at least:

  1. A representative scalar case (single cell, constant forcing).
  2. A vectorized case (multiple cells with varying forcing).
  3. Boundary conditions, especially temperatures near 20 degrees Celsius where the Arrhenius correction is unity, and zero-concentration inputs.

Tolerance selection matters. Pick the loosest tolerance that still detects real regressions. The project uses np.testing.assert_allclose with an explicit rtol. A relative tolerance of 1e-6 is typical when both implementations agree on the rate equation; a looser tolerance is acceptable if the test docstring explains why (for example, when the reference uses single-precision arithmetic). Document the tolerance in the test docstring along with the reason.

def test_tracer_reference_parity_vectorized():
    """Tracer matches the reference within 1e-6 relative tolerance on a 3-cell grid.

    Tolerance chosen to detect any change in the Arrhenius exponent while
    allowing for minor floating-point reordering relative to the reference.
    """
    # ... fixture setup ...
    np.testing.assert_allclose(rate.values, reference_rate, rtol=1e-6)

docs.title: Integration Tests
docs.text:
Integration tests run a full coupled simulation end-to-end. They confirm that the Model loads input data, steps through time, calls every process in the configured order, and writes output to the zarr store without raising. They live under tests/integration/.

Integration tests are slower than unit tests and should use a small reference mesh and a short simulation window. Assert on high-level outputs: that the zarr store contains every requested output variable, that the time axis matches the requested simulation window, and that the output values are finite and non-degenerate.

def test_coupled_run_writes_expected_outputs(tmp_path):
    """Coupled Temperature + FloatingAlgae run writes both outputs to zarr."""
    model = build_test_model(root_directory=tmp_path)
    model.run()

    store = xr.open_zarr(tmp_path / "model_outputs.zarr")
    assert "water_temperature" in store
    assert "algae_floating" in store
    assert np.all(np.isfinite(store["water_temperature"].values))

docs.title: Running Tests Locally
docs.text:
Run the full suite from the repository root.

pytest tests/

Run a single layer, a single file, or a single test.

pytest tests/unit/                                   # all unit tests
pytest tests/parity/test_tsm_parity.py               # one file
pytest tests/unit/tracer/test_rate_decay.py::test_rate_decay_scales_with_concentration

Generate a coverage report.

pytest --cov=clearwater_modules --cov-report=term-missing tests/

Run tests in parallel on multi-core machines, which significantly speeds up the parity suite.

pytest -n auto tests/

docs.title: Continuous Integration Expectations
docs.text:
Every pull request must pass the full test suite in CI before it can be merged. The CI workflow:

  1. Checks out the branch and installs dependencies via pixi.
  2. Runs pytest tests/ with coverage.
  3. Fails the build if any test fails, if overall coverage drops below the configured threshold, or if new code lacks tests.

Pull requests that add a new Process subclass without at least a unit test and a reference-parity test will be sent back for revision. See the Contributing Guidelines for the complete pull request checklist.

Run the suite before pushing

Running pytest tests/ locally before pushing catches most CI failures up front. The full suite on a laptop takes under a minute for unit tests and a few minutes for the integration layer.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
This section collects worked Jupyter notebook examples that demonstrate how to set up, run, and analyze ClearWater simulations. The notebooks are organized into two groups: Tutorials that teach the framework on a small synthetic test case, and a Case Study that demonstrates the transport engine on a real-world domain.

The notebooks are rendered directly from this repository with their committed cell outputs. To run them yourself, install the pinned ClearWater packages (see Installation) and open the corresponding notebook from docs/examples/notebooks/ in JupyterLab. Inputs and precomputed outputs live alongside the notebooks under docs/examples/data/.

docs.title: Tutorials
docs.text:
The tutorial notebooks all use the Willowbend Creek test case, a 2 km by 2 km synthetic lowland stream with a meander bend and an oxbow backwater. Three boundaries drive the domain: a steady upstream inflow, a cool spring-fed tributary at the inside of the meander, and a warmer powerplant discharge into the oxbow. The simulation runs from 2022-05-13 08:00 to 2022-05-14 20:00 UTC at a 30-second time step. All Willowbend tutorials share the inputs in docs/examples/data/willowbend_creek/.

  • Getting Started with Riverine. A first-look tour of the ClearWater-Riverine transport solver. The notebook loads the HEC-RAS 2D plan, configures conservative transport for a single tracer, runs the solver on the computational mesh, and plots the velocity field and tracer concentration over time.

  • Willowbend Creek Temperature. Couples ClearWater-Riverine transport with the Temperature Simulation Module (TSM). The notebook produces the velocity, water-depth, meteorology, spatial-temperature, and time-series-temperature figures from the ClearWater-Riverine Temperature technical report, plus a refugia map and a refugia-persistence time series quantifying cool-water habitat formed by the spring-fed tributary at the meander bend.

  • Willowbend Creek Nutrients. Couples ClearWater-Riverine, TSM, and the Nutrient Simulation Module (NSM1) over the same domain and time window. The notebook produces spatial fields and oxbow time series for the nitrogen, phosphorus, carbon, dissolved-oxygen, and floating-algae state variables, illustrating how the powerplant inflow into the slow-flowing oxbow creates spatially heterogeneous nutrient and DO gradients.

docs.title: Case Studies
docs.text: • Ohio River Transport. A real-world demonstration of the ClearWater-Riverine transport engine on a HEC-RAS 2D model of a reach of the Ohio River. The case study simulates E. coli transport as a conservative tracer and compares the result against a reference EFDC (Environmental Fluid Dynamics Code) simulation of the same domain. Inputs are bundled under docs/examples/data/ohio_river/; the HEC-RAS plan HDF is fetched separately from the source repository (see the README in that directory).

docs.title: Ohio River input data
docs.text: This directory contains the input files used by the Ohio River case-study notebook at docs/examples/notebooks/04_ohio_river_transport.ipynb. The case study demonstrates the ClearWater-Riverine transport engine on a real-world HEC-RAS 2D model and validates the result against an EFDC reference simulation of the same domain.

docs.title: Contents
docs.text: File Purpose cwr_initial_conditions.csv Initial concentration field, one row per HEC-RAS 2D mesh cell cwr_boundary_conditions.csv Boundary concentration time series at each inflow efdc/efdc_ohio_river_model_shapefile/ EFDC model mesh (shapefile) used for plotting the EFDC reference solution efdc/ohio_river-2010.parquet/ EFDC simulated E. coli concentrations on the EFDC mesh, used as the reference for ClearWater-Riverine validation

docs.title: Large files (not committed)
docs.text:
The HEC-RAS 2D plan HDF for this case study is approximately 110 MB and is not committed to this documentation repository. Fetch it from the ClearWater-riverine source repository, which tracks it under git LFS:

git clone https://github.com/EcohydrologyTeam/ClearWater-riverine.git
cd ClearWater-riverine
git lfs pull
cp examples/data/ohio_river/OhioRiver_m.p22.hdf <docs-repo>/docs/examples/data/ohio_river/

After fetching, the directory should contain OhioRiver_m.p22.hdf alongside the files listed above. The notebook checks for this file at startup and prints a clear message pointing back to this README if it is missing.

docs.title: Domain and reference
docs.text: The HEC-RAS 2D model of the Ohio River reach was constructed to mirror an EFDC model of the same domain that simulated E. coli transport as a conservative dye. The two models share the same boundary forcing and broadly similar mesh extent; the case study compares ClearWater-Riverine on the HEC-RAS mesh against the EFDC reference solution to demonstrate that the transport engine reproduces a trusted external solution on a real domain.

docs.title: Willowbend Creek input data
docs.text:
This directory contains the input files and precomputed simulation outputs used by the Willowbend Creek tutorial notebooks under docs/examples/notebooks/.

Willowbend Creek is a 2 km by 2 km synthetic lowland-stream test case with a meander bend and an oxbow backwater. The same case appears in upstream demonstrations under the informal name "Sumwere Creek".

docs.title: Contents
docs.text: File Purpose clearWaterTestCases.p48.hdf HEC-RAS 2D plan HDF, providing mesh topology, face flows, cell volumes, and water-surface elevations cwr_initial_conditions_temp.csv Initial water-temperature field, one row per mesh cell cwr_boundary_conditions_temp.csv Boundary water-temperature time series at each inflow cwr_boundary_conditions_TairC_p28.csv Air-temperature meteorological forcing cwr_boundary_conditions_q_Solar_p28.csv Shortwave-radiation meteorological forcing riverine.yml ClearWater-Riverine transport configuration modules.yml Coupled Riverine + TSM configuration model_inputs.zarr Pre-extracted hydrodynamic and meteorological inputs model_outputs.zarr Precomputed coupled Riverine + TSM simulation output nsm1_output.zarr Precomputed coupled Riverine + TSM + NSM1 simulation output (see note below)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• The simulation runs from 2022-05-13 08:00 to 2022-05-14 20:00 UTC at a 30-second time step.
  • The HEC-RAS plan filename retains its conventional .p48. plan number; this is a HEC-RAS naming convention and does not refer to a particular mesh refinement.
  • The NSM1 simulation output (nsm1_output.zarr) reproduces the figures in the ClearWater-Riverine Nutrients technical report. It is regenerated by running the coupled Riverine + TSM + NSM1 model using modules.yml (with the nsm1 process block enabled). See docs/examples/notebooks/03_willowbend_nutrients.ipynb for the configuration and a one-cell command to regenerate this file.

docs.text:

docs.title: Getting Started: 2D Conservative Transport on the Willowbend Creek Mesh¶
docs.text:
This notebook is a first-look tour of the ClearWater-Riverine transport solver. It loads the Willowbend Creek HEC-RAS 2D plan, configures a single conservative tracer, runs the solver on the computational mesh, and produces velocity and concentration plots.

Willowbend Creek is a 2 km by 2 km synthetic lowland stream with a meander bend and an oxbow backwater. Three boundaries drive the domain: a steady upstream inflow, a cool spring-fed tributary at the inside of the meander, and a powerplant discharge into the oxbow. Inputs and a precomputed simulation output are bundled under docs/examples/data/willowbend_creek/.

docs.title: 1. Imports and paths¶
docs.text: Run this notebook from the documentation repository root. The relative path docs/examples/data/willowbend_creek/ must resolve to the bundled test-case directory.

docs.title: 2. Load the transport configuration and run the model¶
docs.text: riverine.yml declares the simulation directory, the HEC-RAS 2D plan HDF, the simulation start and end times, the time step, the chunk size, the diffusion coefficient, and the constituents to transport. The bundled configuration carries a single tracer constituent with constant initial and boundary values, which keeps the demonstration focused on the transport engine itself.

docs.title: 3. Open the simulation output¶
docs.text: model.run() writes the simulated state to a zarr store referenced from riverine.yml. The bundled model_outputs.zarr is the same store written by a previous run and can be opened directly with xarray.

docs.title: 4. Plot the velocity field on the computational mesh¶
docs.text: The HEC-RAS 2D solution provides a face-averaged flow on every internal edge of the unstructured mesh. The cell-averaged velocity is reconstructed from the face flows and plotted below as a quiver overlay on the mesh.

docs.title: 5. Plot tracer concentration at representative cells¶
docs.text: The bundled tracer constituent is initialized at 100 throughout the domain and held at 100 at every boundary, so a conservative-transport solution should remain near 100 everywhere. Departures from 100 indicate numerical diffusion or boundary-flux artifacts and are useful for sanity-checking a new mesh or a new boundary configuration.

docs.title: 6. Plot the tracer field at end of simulation¶
Next steps¶
docs.text:
• Couple the transport solver to the Temperature Simulation Module (TSM): see Willowbend Creek Temperature.
  • Add the Nutrient Simulation Module (NSM1) to a coupled run: see Willowbend Creek Nutrients.
  • Apply the transport engine to a real-world domain: see Ohio River Transport.

def face_polygons(registry):
    # Return a list of (Nvert x 2) polygon vertex arrays, one per real cell,
    # plus the corresponding face index for each polygon. Cells whose
    # face_nodes row contains fewer than three valid node references are
    # skipped (this happens for ghost/padding rows in the HDF).
    nx = registry.get("node_x").values
    ny = registry.get("node_y").values
    face_nodes = registry.get("face_nodes").values
    n_nodes = len(nx)
    polys, face_ids = [], []
    for i in range(face_nodes.shape[0]):
        row = face_nodes[i]
        mask = np.isfinite(row) & (row >= 0) & (row < n_nodes)
        nodes = row[mask].astype(int)
        if len(nodes) < 3:
            continue
        polys.append(np.column_stack([nx[nodes], ny[nodes]]))
        face_ids.append(i)
    return polys, np.array(face_ids)


def plot_polygons(ax, polys, face_ids, values, *, cmap="viridis", norm=None,
                  vmin=None, vmax=None, mask=None,
                  show_edges=False, edgecolor="k", lw=0.2):
    # Shade each cell polygon by its per-face value. Cells where mask==False
    # are drawn with the dry/inactive style; wet cells are colored from the
    # colormap. Returns a ScalarMappable suitable for fig.colorbar().
    values = np.asarray(values).squeeze()
    if values.ndim > 1:
        values = values[..., 0]
    vals = values[face_ids]
    if mask is not None:
        mask_arr = np.asarray(mask).squeeze()
        if mask_arr.ndim > 1:
            mask_arr = mask_arr[..., 0]
        cell_mask = mask_arr[face_ids].astype(bool)
    else:
        cell_mask = np.ones(len(face_ids), dtype=bool)
    finite_vals = vals[cell_mask & np.isfinite(vals)]
    if norm is None:
        if vmin is None:
            vmin = float(np.nanmin(finite_vals)) if finite_vals.size else 0.0
        if vmax is None:
            vmax = float(np.nanmax(finite_vals)) if finite_vals.size else 1.0
        if vmin == vmax:
            vmax = vmin + max(1e-9, abs(vmin) * 1e-3)
        norm = Normalize(vmin=vmin, vmax=vmax)
    cmap_obj = plt.get_cmap(cmap) if isinstance(cmap, str) else cmap
    data_colors = cmap_obj(norm(np.clip(vals, norm.vmin, norm.vmax)))

    dry = [polys[i] for i in range(len(polys)) if not cell_mask[i]]
    if dry:
        ax.add_collection(PatchCollection(
            [MplPolygon(p, closed=True) for p in dry],
            facecolors=DRY_FILL, edgecolors="none",
        ))
    wet = [polys[i] for i in range(len(polys)) if cell_mask[i]]
    wet_colors = np.array([data_colors[i]
                           for i in range(len(polys)) if cell_mask[i]])
    if wet:
        ax.add_collection(PatchCollection(
            [MplPolygon(p, closed=True) for p in wet],
            facecolors=wet_colors,
            edgecolors="none",
        ))
    # Overlay consistent grid-cell outlines on top of the fills so the
    # mesh is visible over both wet and dry cells. Uses the dry-cell
    # outline color for a uniform look across every plot.
    outline_color = edgecolor if show_edges else DRY_EDGE
    outline_lw = lw if show_edges else 0.15
    ax.add_collection(PatchCollection(
        [MplPolygon(p, closed=True) for p in polys],
        facecolors="none", edgecolors=outline_color, linewidths=outline_lw,
        zorder=3,
    ))
    sm = plt.cm.ScalarMappable(cmap=cmap_obj, norm=norm)
    sm.set_array([])
    return sm


def set_common_axis(ax, face_x_da, face_y_da, pad=50):
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.set_xlim(float(face_x_da.min()) - pad, float(face_x_da.max()) + pad)
    ax.set_ylim(float(face_y_da.min()) - pad, float(face_y_da.max()) + pad)
    ax.set_xlabel("UTM Easting (m)")
    ax.set_ylabel("UTM Northing (m)")

# Boundary-condition cell lookup. Registry exposes per-boundary-edge arrays
# "Name", "Face Index" (edge index in the HEC-RAS sense), and "BC Line ID".
# Each edge is resolved to an adjacent real cell via edge_face_connectivity.
LABEL_MAP = {
    "US_Flow": "Upstream inflow (15 degC)",
    "CoriolisColdSpringCreek": "Cold-water spring (10 degC)",
    "PwrPlnt_Flow": "Power plant outfall (20-25 degC)",
    "DS_Stage": "Downstream stage",
}


def _boundary_cells(registry) -> dict[str, list[int]]:
    try:
        names = registry.get("Name").values
        edge_idx = registry.get("Face Index").values.astype(int)
        efc = registry.get("edge_face_connectivity").values.astype(int)
    except (KeyError, ValueError):
        return {}
    nface = face_x.size
    out: dict[str, list[int]] = {}
    for name in np.unique(names):
        sel = (names == name)
        edges = edge_idx[sel]
        cs = []
        for e in edges:
            adj = efc[e]
            cand = [c for c in adj if 0 <= c < nface]
            if cand:
                cs.append(cand[0])
        if cs:
            out[str(name)] = sorted(set(cs))
    return out

for i, (raw_label, cs) in enumerate(bc_cells.items()):
    color = bc_colors[i % len(bc_colors)]
    friendly = LABEL_MAP.get(raw_label, raw_label)
    bc_polys = [face_id_to_poly[c] for c in cs if c in face_id_to_poly]

def _cell_velocity_at(time_idx):
    es = np.abs(registry.get("edge_velocity").isel(time=time_idx).values)
    csum = np.zeros(nface)
    ccnt = np.zeros(nface, dtype=int)
    for e in range(edge_face_conn.shape[0]):
        s = es[e]
        if not np.isfinite(s):
            continue
        for c in edge_face_conn[e]:
            if 0 <= c < nface:
                csum[c] += s
                ccnt[c] += 1
    return np.where(ccnt > 0, csum / np.maximum(ccnt, 1), 0.0)
