    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 5.2))
    ax = axes[0]
    ch_mask = regions["channel"]
    ox_mask = regions["oxbow"]
    other_mask = active & ~ch_mask & ~ox_mask
    ax.scatter(ap_mean[other_mask], do_amp[other_mask], s=18, c="#9ec9e0",
               label="floodplain margin", edgecolors="none")
    ax.scatter(ap_mean[ch_mask], do_amp[ch_mask], s=22, c="#d62728",
               label="main channel", edgecolors="none")
    ax.scatter(ap_mean[ox_mask], do_amp[ox_mask], s=28, c="#2ca02c",
               label="oxbow", edgecolors="none")
    ax.set_xlabel(r"mean A$_p$ ($\mu$g-Chl-a/L)")
    ax.set_ylabel(r"DO diurnal amplitude (mg-O$_2$/L)")
    ax.set_title("(a) Chlorophyll-a vs. DO diurnal amplitude")
    ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
    ax.legend()

    ax = axes[1]
    ox_ap = ds["Ap"].isel(nface=np.where(ox_mask)[0]).mean(dim="nface").values
    ox_do = ds["DOX"].isel(nface=np.where(ox_mask)[0]).mean(dim="nface").values
    l1, = ax.plot(th, ox_do, lw=1.6, color="#1f77b4", label="DO (left axis)")
    ax.set_xlabel("hours from start")
    ax.set_ylabel(r"DO (mg-O$_2$/L)", color="#1f77b4")
    ax.tick_params(axis="y", labelcolor="#1f77b4")
    ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
    ax2 = ax.twinx()
    l2, = ax2.plot(th, ox_ap, lw=1.6, color="#2ca02c", label=r"A$_p$ (right axis)")
    ax2.set_ylabel(r"A$_p$ ($\mu$g-Chl-a/L)", color="#2ca02c")
    ax2.tick_params(axis="y", labelcolor="#2ca02c")
    ax.set_title(r"(b) Oxbow-averaged DO and A$_p$")
    ax.legend([l1, l2], [l1.get_label(), l2.get_label()], loc="best")

    fig.suptitle("Algae-DO coupling", fontsize=11)
    fig.tight_layout()
    return fig
def fig_algae_do_coupling(ds, regions): active = regions["active"] do = ds["DOX"].values ap = ds["Ap"].values do_amp = np.nanmax(do, axis=0) - np.nanmin(do, axis=0) ap_mean = np.nanmean(ap, axis=0) t = ds["time"].values th = (t - t[0]) / np.timedelta64(1, "h") fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 5.2)) ax = axes[0] ch_mask = regions["channel"] ox_mask = regions["oxbow"] other_mask = active & ~ch_mask & ~ox_mask ax.scatter(ap_mean[other_mask], do_amp[other_mask], s=18, c="#9ec9e0", label="floodplain margin", edgecolors="none") ax.scatter(ap_mean[ch_mask], do_amp[ch_mask], s=22, c="#d62728", label="main channel", edgecolors="none") ax.scatter(ap_mean[ox_mask], do_amp[ox_mask], s=28, c="#2ca02c", label="oxbow", edgecolors="none") ax.set_xlabel(r"mean A$_p$ ($\mu$g-Chl-a/L)") ax.set_ylabel(r"DO diurnal amplitude (mg-O$_2$/L)") ax.set_title("(a) Chlorophyll-a vs. DO diurnal amplitude") ax.grid(alpha=0.3) ax.legend() ax = axes[1] ox_ap = ds["Ap"].isel(nface=np.where(ox_mask)[0]).mean(dim="nface").values ox_do = ds["DOX"].isel(nface=np.where(ox_mask)[0]).mean(dim="nface").values l1, = ax.plot(th, ox_do, lw=1.6, color="#1f77b4", label="DO (left axis)") ax.set_xlabel("hours from start") ax.set_ylabel(r"DO (mg-O$_2$/L)", color="#1f77b4") ax.tick_params(axis="y", labelcolor="#1f77b4") ax.grid(alpha=0.3) ax2 = ax.twinx() l2, = ax2.plot(th, ox_ap, lw=1.6, color="#2ca02c", label=r"A$_p$ (right axis)") ax2.set_ylabel(r"A$_p$ ($\mu$g-Chl-a/L)", color="#2ca02c") ax2.tick_params(axis="y", labelcolor="#2ca02c") ax.set_title(r"(b) Oxbow-averaged DO and A$_p$") ax.legend([l1, l2], [l1.get_label(), l2.get_label()], loc="best") fig.suptitle("Algae-DO coupling", fontsize=11) fig.tight_layout() return fig

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
This section introduces the ClearWater framework and walks new users from installation through a first coupled simulation. The Getting Started pages assume a working knowledge of Python and scientific computing with numpy and xarray, but they do not assume prior experience with HEC-RAS or water quality modeling.

Start with the Overview to understand how the three ClearWater packages fit together, then follow the Installation guide to set up a working environment. The Quickstart tutorial walks through a minimal end-to-end simulation that couples ClearWater-Riverine with the Temperature Simulation Module (TSM).

docs.title: Contents
docs.text:
• Overview -- Architecture of the ClearWater framework, the three-package design, and the Process-based execution model.
  • Installation -- Prerequisites, environment setup, and installation from source for each of the three ClearWater packages.
  • Quickstart -- A minimal tutorial that configures, runs, and inspects the results of a coupled Riverine plus TSM simulation.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: This page describes how to install the three ClearWater packages. Released packages can be installed from PyPI or conda-forge for routine use, or from source for development.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
ClearWater requires the following:

  • Python 3.11 or later.
  • A Python environment manager. We recommend pixi for reproducible, lockfile-driven installs, or Miniconda / Mamba for traditional conda workflows.
  • Git, if installing from source.
  • A working installation of HEC-RAS 2D (Hydrologic Engineering Center's River Analysis System, Windows) or a pre-computed HEC-RAS plan HDF file, if you plan to use ClearWater-Riverine. ClearWater itself runs on Linux, macOS, and Windows.

conda installation location

If you choose Miniconda or Anaconda, install it in your local user directory. System-wide installs create persistent permission problems when creating environments.

docs.title: Install with pixi (recommended)
docs.text:
Each ClearWater repository ships a pixi.toml and a committed pixi.lock. Pixi resolves all dependencies from conda-forge and PyPI together, produces a fully reproducible environment, and does not require a separate conda installation.

git clone https://github.com/EcohydrologyTeam/ClearWater-modules.git
cd ClearWater-modules
pixi install
pixi shell

Inside the pixi shell, the clearwater_modules, clearwater_riverine, and clearwater_data packages are available alongside JupyterLab and the visualization stack. Use pixi run jupyter lab to start JupyterLab without entering a shell.

docs.title: Install with conda or mamba
docs.text:
If you prefer conda, create a single environment from ClearWater-modules/environment.yml and install all three packages into it:

git clone https://github.com/EcohydrologyTeam/ClearWater-modules.git
git clone https://github.com/EcohydrologyTeam/ClearWater-riverine.git
git clone https://github.com/EcohydrologyTeam/ClearWater-data.git

cd ClearWater-modules
conda env create --file environment.yml --solver=libmamba
conda activate ClearWater-modules

pip install -e ../ClearWater-data
pip install -e ../ClearWater-riverine
pip install -e ../ClearWater-modules

The libmamba solver is substantially faster than the classic conda solver. The pip install -e order matters because clearwater_modules and clearwater_riverine both depend on clearwater_data; install clearwater_data first.

docs.title: Install from PyPI
docs.text:
Released versions are published to PyPI and can be installed into any Python 3.11+ environment:

pip install clearwater-data clearwater-riverine clearwater-modules

For a quick read-only install (for example, on a teaching cluster), this is the simplest path. For development work or for running the example notebooks against the latest commits, install from source as shown above.

docs.title: Verify the Installation
docs.text:
Confirm that each package imports cleanly and reports a version string:

python -c "import clearwater_data; print(clearwater_data.__version__)"
python -c "import clearwater_riverine; print(clearwater_riverine.__version__)"
python -c "import clearwater_modules; print(clearwater_modules.__version__)"

To verify that the test suites pass, run pytest from each repository root:

pixi run pytest    # or, in a conda environment:
pytest

docs.title: Jupyter and Example Notebooks
docs.text:
The example notebooks in each repository's examples/ directory depend on JupyterLab and the visualization stack that ships with the standard environment. Start JupyterLab from a pixi shell or activated conda environment:

jupyter lab

The lckr-jupyterlab-variableinspector extension is useful for inspecting live xarray and numpy objects during interactive development.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Plots not displaying in notebooks

The ClearWater-riverine repository ships a fallback environment_working.yml that pins specific versions of the holoviews/hvplot visualization stack. If plots fail to render after upgrading a host system, recreate the environment from this fallback file:

conda env create -f environment_working.yml --solver=libmamba

No Fortran compiler is required

ClearWater-Modules is pure Python; no Fortran compiler is needed. If a package fails to build with a Fortran-related error, confirm that pip is installing from the ClearWater repositories or from PyPI rather than from an unrelated package with a similar name.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: ClearWater is a Python framework for coupled hydrodynamic and water quality modeling. The framework is designed around the idea that transport and reaction kinetics are separable concerns: a transport engine moves mass through a mesh, and a set of independent process modules compute the sources and sinks that modify constituent concentrations at each cell. This section describes the three packages that make up ClearWater, the Process-based architecture that governs how kinetics are computed, the chunked data layer that enables long simulations, and the HEC-RAS coupling that drives the transport grid.

docs.title: The Three Packages
docs.text:
ClearWater is distributed as three Python packages that are developed and versioned independently but are designed to be composed into a full simulation.

ClearWater-Riverine is a two-dimensional (2D) transport engine. ClearWater-Riverine reads HEC-RAS (Hydrologic Engineering Center's River Analysis System) 2D HDF output, extracts the unstructured mesh geometry, face flows, cell volumes, and water surface elevations, and solves the advection-diffusion equation for an arbitrary number of constituents. ClearWater-Riverine assumes vertical homogeneity, so the model is best suited for riverine and estuarine systems where longitudinal and lateral gradients dominate over vertical stratification.

ClearWater-Modules provides the water quality reaction kinetics. The package ships the Temperature Simulation Module (TSM), the General Constituent Simulation Module (GSM), and the Nutrient Simulation Module (NSM1, with sixteen state variables spanning the nitrogen, phosphorus, and carbon cycles, algae, dissolved oxygen, CBOD, particulate organic matter, pathogens, and alkalinity). Each module computes the net reaction rate for its state variables at each mesh cell and time step; the resulting source/sink term is applied by the transport engine during integration.

ClearWater-Data is the data layer. ClearWater-Data provides a VariableRegistry abstraction that manages state variables across time and mesh dimensions, together with a ChunkedZarrDataStore that backs the registry with a zarr store on disk. This layer decouples the model state from Python process memory, which is the foundation for long-duration simulations.

docs.title: Process-Based Architecture
docs.text:
ClearWater is built on a unified Process abstract base class. Each kinetic module (temperature, floating algae, benthic algae, nitrogen, and so on) is implemented as a Process subclass that declares its required inputs, produced outputs, and configuration schema. The framework provides a ProcessFactory that instantiates processes from YAML configuration files, and a Model class that orchestrates the run.

Each Process has a three-phase lifecycle:

  1. init_process -- The process initializes its internal state, reads its configuration, and registers its variables with the VariableRegistry.
  2. run(time, registry) -- The process reads the current state from the registry, computes its kinetic source/sink terms, and writes updated values back to the registry at the specified time index.
  3. finalize_process -- The process releases resources and flushes any buffered output.

This design makes it possible to add new water quality processes without modifying the transport engine or the data layer, and it enforces explicit coupling between processes via the VariableRegistry rather than through shared Python objects.

docs.title: Chunked Zarr Data Layer
docs.text:
Long water quality simulations can produce output volumes that exceed available RAM, particularly when many constituents are simulated on fine meshes over multi-year periods. ClearWater addresses this through the ChunkedZarrDataStore, which stores simulation state as a chunked zarr array on disk. The VariableRegistry reads and writes state at a specific time index on demand via get_at_time() and set_at_time(), so only the currently active chunks are resident in memory.

This architecture enables out-of-core time stepping, where the model streams through a long simulation without holding the full time history in RAM, and it produces a self-describing xarray-compatible output dataset that can be analyzed incrementally.

docs.title: HEC-RAS Coupling
docs.text:
ClearWater-Riverine couples to HEC-RAS 2D as a post-processor on the HEC-RAS hydrodynamic solution. A typical workflow runs an unsteady HEC-RAS 2D simulation to produce a plan HDF file, then ClearWater-Riverine reads the HDF file to extract the mesh topology and the time series of face-averaged flows, cell volumes, and water surface elevations. ClearWater-Riverine then solves the transport equation on the HEC-RAS mesh using the HEC-RAS time step, and the ClearWater-Modules processes compute reaction kinetics at each step.

Because ClearWater reads HEC-RAS output rather than running inside HEC-RAS, users can leverage existing HEC-RAS 2D models of rivers, reservoirs, and floodplains for water quality studies without reconfiguring or re-running the hydrodynamic solution.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
This quickstart walks through a minimal coupled simulation that uses ClearWater-Riverine for 2D transport and the Temperature Simulation Module (TSM) from ClearWater-Modules for water temperature kinetics. The example assumes you have completed the Installation steps. It uses the Willowbend Creek synthetic test case bundled with the documentation under docs/examples/data/willowbend_creek/.

The full worked example, with all boundary-condition inputs, plotting code, and committed figure outputs, is available as a Jupyter notebook at examples/notebooks/02_willowbend_temperature.ipynb. This page summarizes the essential steps.

docs.title: 1. Activate the Environment and Import Packages
docs.text:
Activate the pixi shell or conda environment created during installation, then launch JupyterLab or start a Python session:

pixi shell
jupyter lab

In a new notebook or script, import the data layer, the transport engine, and the model orchestrator:

from pathlib import Path

import xarray as xr

from clearwater_modules import Model

docs.title: 2. Point at the Bundled Willowbend Inputs
docs.text:
The Willowbend Creek test case ships with a HEC-RAS 2D plan HDF, boundary-condition CSVs, meteorological forcing CSVs, and two YAML configuration files (riverine.yml for transport-only and modules.yml for coupled Riverine + TSM):

data_dir = Path("docs/examples/data/willowbend_creek")
config_path = data_dir / "modules.yml"

assert (data_dir / "clearWaterTestCases.p48.hdf").exists()
assert config_path.exists()

The modules.yml file declares the simulation start and end times (2022-05-13 08:00 to 2022-05-14 20:00), the time step (30 seconds), the chunk time step for streaming output (36 hours), the list of output variables, and the processes to run.

docs.title: 3. Build the Model from YAML
docs.text:
The Model.from_config constructor instantiates the Process objects, wires up the shared VariableRegistry, and prepares the chunked zarr data store for output:

model = Model.from_config(config_path)

At this point the model has parsed every process configuration, opened the HEC-RAS 2D plan, and validated the boundary-condition and meteorological forcing files. Configuration errors (missing fields, unknown providers, out-of-range parameters) are reported here before any time stepping begins.

docs.title: 4. Run the Coupled Simulation
docs.text:
Model.run advances the simulation from the configured start time to the configured end time, writing each output chunk to the zarr store referenced in modules.yml:

model.run()

For a long simulation, Model.run streams chunks to disk through the ChunkedZarrDataStore. Only the currently active chunk is held in memory.

docs.title: 5. Inspect the Results
docs.text:
Open the output store as an xarray.Dataset and plot a time series at a cell of interest:

results = xr.open_zarr(data_dir / "model_outputs.zarr")

print(results)
print(results["water_temperature"].mean(dim="nface").to_pandas().head())

results["water_temperature"].isel(nface=1250).plot()

The output store contains the full simulated state on the original HEC-RAS unstructured mesh. Use standard xarray operations to compute spatial statistics, extract transects, or produce animations.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
• Explore the Willowbend Creek Temperature notebook for a full walkthrough that produces the figures from the ClearWater-Riverine Temperature technical report.
  • Try the Willowbend Creek Nutrients notebook to add the Nutrient Simulation Module (NSM1) to a coupled run.
  • Read the Overview for a conceptual description of the Process-based architecture and the chunked data layer.

docs.title: Release Notes
docs.text: This page summarizes notable changes between releases of the three ClearWater packages: clearwater_data, clearwater_riverine, and clearwater_modules. Versions are coordinated across packages so that a given combination is known to be tested together.

docs.title: 1.0.0 -- Released ClearWater Framework
docs.text: This is the first coordinated stable release of the ClearWater framework, replacing the experimental _v2 namespace used during the architectural refactor. The release consolidates the three packages on a single Process abstract base class, a chunked zarr data layer, and YAML-driven model assembly.

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text:
• Unified Process ABC. Every kinetic module (TSM, GSM, every NSM1 process) is now a Process subclass with explicit init_process / run / finalize_process lifecycle hooks. The clearwater_modules_v2 development namespace has been merged into clearwater_modules; only one import path exists.
  • Optimized NSM1. All sixteen NSM1 state variables (NH4, NO3, OrgN, N2, TIP, OrgP, POC, DOC, DIC, DOX, CBOD, Ap, Ab, Alk, POM, PX) are vectorized over the unstructured-mesh dimension using broadcast xarray operations. Reaction-kinetic kernels run roughly two times faster than the original Fortran-derived port, and peak memory is reduced by approximately thirty percent on representative cases. See the Theory page and the ClearWater-Riverine optimization paper for benchmarks.
  • Chunked, out-of-core simulation. clearwater_data ships VariableRegistry and ChunkedZarrDataStore as the canonical state container. get_at_time() and set_at_time() provide time-indexed access that streams chunks from disk, so multi-year, fine-mesh runs no longer require holding the full simulation history in RAM.
  • HEC-RAS 2D coupling stabilized. clearwater_riverine reads HEC-RAS 2D plan HDF files directly, extracts mesh topology and the time series of cell volumes, face flows, and water surface elevations, and integrates the depth-averaged advection-diffusion equation on the native HEC-RAS unstructured mesh.
  • YAML model assembly. A single modules.yml declares the simulation directory, time window, processes, and per-process configuration. The ProcessFactory instantiates processes from this configuration and registers them with the transport engine.
  • Reproducible installs. Every repository ships a pixi.toml with a committed pixi.lock. PyPI and conda-forge packaging is in place for routine installs.

docs.title: Demonstrations
docs.text:
The release ships two reference demonstrations on the Willowbend Creek synthetic test case (a 2 km by 2 km lowland stream with a meander bend and oxbow backwater, originally introduced in the upstream ClearWater-Riverine demos as "Sumwere Creek"):

  • Thermal refugia in the meander bend -- a TSM-only run that quantifies cool-water refugia formed by a spring-fed tributary at the inside of a meander, including a refugia map and persistence-time analysis. This demonstration accompanies the ClearWater-Riverine Temperature technical report.
  • Algal, nutrient, and DO gradients in the oxbow lake -- a coupled Riverine + TSM + NSM1 run that resolves spatially heterogeneous nitrogen, phosphorus, dissolved-oxygen, and floating-algae fields driven by a powerplant-discharge inflow into a slow-flowing oxbow. This demonstration accompanies the ClearWater-Riverine Nutrients technical report.

Both demonstrations are reproducible from the publication notebooks in the Publication-ClearWater-Riverine-01-Temperature/notebooks/ and Publication-ClearWater-Riverine-02-Nutrients/notebooks/ directories.

docs.title: Breaking changes
docs.text:
• The clearwater_modules_v2 import path has been removed. Update imports from clearwater_modules_v2.processes... to the corresponding clearwater_modules.processes... path.
  • Latent-heat-of-vaporization fixes that were applied as patches in the publication notebooks are now part of the released TSM kinetics. Custom user wrappers that re-converted Celsius inputs to Kelvin should be removed.
  • Earlier sentinel placeholder values (such as 999) for several NSM1 parameters have been replaced with realistic, documented defaults. Users who previously set these parameters explicitly should see no change; users who relied on package defaults should re-read the NSM1 parameter pages.

docs.title: Known issues
docs.text:
• ClearWater-Riverine assumes vertical homogeneity and does not represent stratification. Reservoir applications with strong thermal stratification are out of scope; pair ClearWater-Modules with CE-QUAL-W2 instead.
  • HEC-RAS 2D coupling is one-way (post-processor on the hydrodynamic solution). Two-way feedback (for example, density-driven flow that depends on the water-quality state) is not supported.

docs.title: Acknowledgments
docs.text: ClearWater is developed by the Environmental Modeling Team at the U.S. Army Engineer Research and Development Center (ERDC), Environmental Laboratory. Substantial contributions to the Process-based architecture, the optimized NSM1 kinetics, and the chunked data layer were made by ERDC and LimnoTech under the ANSRP and ESM programs.

docs.title: Theory
docs.text: This section presents the theoretical foundations of the ClearWater framework. The pages here describe the governing equations, physical assumptions, and numerical techniques shared across the kinetic modules. Refer back to these pages from the module-specific user guide when you need the derivation or physical justification behind a particular rate or flux expression.

docs.title: In This Section
docs.text:
• Hydrodynamics summarizes the role of the external transport model and the scope of what ClearWater itself computes.
  • Temperature presents the surface energy balance used by TSM.
  • Kinetics documents the Arrhenius temperature correction, Monod / Michaelis-Menten limitation, stoichiometric ratios, and first-order decay formulations used across NSM1 and GSM.
  • Numerical Methods describes the explicit Euler time integration, positivity clipping, and chunked execution pattern.

docs.title: Hydrodynamics
docs.text: ClearWater is a water quality kinetics framework. It does not solve the shallow-water equations, the Navier-Stokes equations, or any hydrodynamic transport. Instead, ClearWater couples to an external hydrodynamic model that supplies velocity fields, depths, volumes, and transport fluxes at each time step. The kinetic modules (TSM, NSM1, GSM, CSM, MSM) then operate on each cell to compute the local source, sink, and reaction terms.

docs.title: Separation of Concerns
docs.text:
The ClearWater design separates two concerns that are often conflated in legacy water quality models:

  • Transport (advection, dispersion, exchange across cell faces) is handled by the hydrodynamic model.
  • Kinetics (biogeochemical reactions, heat fluxes, settling) is handled by the ClearWater modules.

Each time step, the hydrodynamic model transports the constituent fields; ClearWater then applies the cell-local kinetic tendencies. This operator-splitting approach is standard in coupled water quality modeling and keeps the kinetic modules independent of any particular hydrodynamic grid or solver.

docs.title: Supported Coupling: ClearWater-Riverine and HEC-RAS 2D
docs.text:
The current reference coupling is to HEC-RAS 2D through the ClearWater-Riverine package. In this configuration:

  • HEC-RAS 2D provides cell geometry, water depths, volumes, face velocities, and inter-cell transport fluxes from a pre-computed unsteady hydraulics run.
  • ClearWater-Riverine advances the transport of each tracked constituent on the 2D mesh at each time step.
  • TSM, NSM1, and the other modules compute the cell-local kinetic tendencies and update the state variables.

HEC-RAS 2D is run to completion first; ClearWater then reads the hydrodynamic output and advances water quality offline. This one-way coupling is appropriate for water quality studies because biogeochemistry does not affect the hydrodynamic solution at the scales of interest.

docs.title: Extending to Other Transport Models
docs.text: Because ClearWater modules interact with the transport solver only through the data registry (see ClearWater-Data), the same kinetic code can be coupled to other transport frameworks. Any model that can supply water depth, cell volume, water temperature forcing, and a time-stepping harness can drive ClearWater. Historical couplings include CE-QUAL-W2, GSSHA, and AdH in their original Fortran implementations.

docs.title: Practical Implications for Users
docs.text:
• Run the hydrodynamic model first and verify its outputs (depths, velocities, mass balance) before launching ClearWater.
  • Use the hydrodynamic time step, or a coarser multiple of it, as the ClearWater kinetic time step. Kinetic time steps finer than the hydrodynamic output resolution provide no additional accuracy.
  • Boundary conditions for water quality constituents (inflow concentrations, point loads) are applied through the transport model, not directly in the kinetic modules.

docs.title: Water Quality Kinetics
docs.text: Every reactive process in ClearWater is expressed as a cell-local rate that depends on water temperature, limiting resources, and stoichiometric conversion factors. This page describes the four kinetic formulations that recur throughout the ClearWater modules: Arrhenius temperature correction, Monod / Michaelis-Menten limitation, fixed stoichiometric ratios, and first-order decay.

docs.title: Arrhenius Temperature Correction
docs.text:
Biological and chemical rate constants depend strongly on water temperature. ClearWater applies the standard Arrhenius-form correction:

\[ r(T) = r_{20} \, \theta^{T - 20} \]

where:

  • \(r(T)\) is the rate constant at water temperature \(T\) (degrees C).
  • \(r_{20}\) is the rate constant at the reference temperature of 20 degrees C.
  • \(\theta\) is the dimensionless temperature coefficient (typically 1.02 to 1.10 for aquatic rate processes).

The value of \(\theta\) encodes how strongly a process responds to temperature. A value of 1.047 (common for many nitrification and mineralization rates) implies the rate roughly doubles for every 15 degrees C increase.

Warning

The Arrhenius formulation is extremely sensitive to unrealistic values of \(\theta\). A \(\theta\) of 999 would grow by many orders of magnitude per degree; a \(\theta\) of 0 would collapse the rate to zero everywhere except at 20 degrees C. Always verify \(\theta\) is a physically reasonable value (typically between 1.0 and 1.15) before running a simulation.

docs.title: Monod / Michaelis-Menten Limitation
docs.text:
When a process depends on a limiting substrate (for example, algal growth limited by nitrogen or phosphorus), ClearWater uses Monod kinetics:

\[ f(S) = \frac{S}{K_s + S} \]

where:

  • \(S\) is the substrate concentration.
  • \(K_s\) is the half-saturation constant; at \(S = K_s\) the limitation factor equals 0.5.

The limitation factor \(f(S)\) ranges from 0 (complete limitation) to 1 (no limitation). When multiple resources (for example, light, nitrogen, phosphorus) independently limit a process, the combined limitation may be taken as the minimum of the individual factors (Liebig's law) or as a multiplicative product, depending on the specific formulation.

docs.title: Inhibition
docs.text:
The same functional form is used with a sign change to represent inhibition by a solute. For example, nitrification is inhibited at low dissolved oxygen through:

\[ f_{\text{inhib}}(\text{DOX}) = \frac{\text{DOX}}{K_{\text{nit}} + \text{DOX}} \]

which approaches 0 at low oxygen and 1 at high oxygen.

docs.title: Stoichiometric Ratios
docs.text:
Reactions that convert between state variables (for example, algal growth converting NH4 into algal biomass) are governed by fixed stoichiometric ratios. NSM1 parameterizes algal stoichiometry as mass ratios of the form:

Parameter Description Default AWd Dry mass to chlorophyll-a 100 AWc Carbon to chlorophyll-a 40 AWn Nitrogen to chlorophyll-a 7.2 AWp Phosphorus to chlorophyll-a 1 AWa Oxygen to chlorophyll-a (photosynthesis) 1000

When the algal growth rate is applied, the same mass flux is subtracted from the nutrient pools in the ratios AWn : AWc : AWp and released to the dissolved oxygen pool in the ratio AWa. Benthic algae use an analogous set of ratios (BWd, BWc, BWn, BWp, BWa).

The Redfield ratio (C:N:P = 106:16:1 by moles) is the conceptual basis for these stoichiometric coefficients, but NSM1 exposes them as tunable parameters to support site-specific calibration.

docs.title: First-Order Decay
docs.text:
The simplest reactive formulation is first-order decay, used for carbonaceous biochemical oxygen demand (CBOD) oxidation, pathogen die-off, GSM generic constituents, and many hydrolysis and mineralization processes:

\[ \frac{\partial C}{\partial t} = -k(T) \, C \]

where \(k(T)\) is the Arrhenius-corrected rate constant (day\(^{-1}\)). The analytical solution in a closed system is exponential decay:

\[ C(t) = C_0 \, e^{-k(T) \, t} \]

First-order decay is an appropriate approximation when the decaying species is far below any saturating threshold for its consumer or catalyst.

docs.title: Combining the Formulations
docs.text:
NSM1 rate expressions typically combine all four elements. For example, the floating algal growth rate takes the form:

\[ \mu = \mu_{\max,20} \, \theta^{T-20} \, \min\left[ f_L, \frac{N}{K_{sN} + N}, \frac{P}{K_{sP} + P} \right] \]

and the nitrogen uptake rate is:

\[ \frac{\partial \text{NH4}}{\partial t} \bigg|_{\text{uptake}} = - \mu \, A_p \, \text{AWn} \cdot P_N \]

where \(P_N\) is the ammonia preference factor that partitions uptake between NH4 and NO3. This pattern (temperature-corrected maximum rate times minimum-of-limitations times stoichiometric conversion) recurs throughout the module.

docs.title: Related Pages
docs.text:
• NSM1 Overview for how these formulations combine into the full 13-variable nutrient model.
  • GSM Configuration for first-order decay applied to user-defined constituents.
  • Numerical Methods for the time integration scheme used to advance these rates.

docs.title: Numerical Methods
docs.text: ClearWater advances its kinetic state variables in time using explicit Euler integration, applies positivity clipping to prevent negative concentrations, and processes large grids in chunks that align with the ClearWater-Data storage backend. This page describes each of these techniques and the reasoning behind them.

docs.title: Explicit Euler Time Integration
docs.text:
Each state variable \(C\) is advanced from time \(t_n\) to \(t_{n+1} = t_n + \Delta t\) by:

\[ C_{n+1} = C_n + \Delta t \, \left. \frac{\partial C}{\partial t} \right|_n \]

where the right-hand-side tendency is evaluated entirely from quantities known at time \(t_n\). Explicit Euler is first-order accurate in time and requires no implicit solve. ClearWater uses this scheme for three reasons:

  • Simplicity. Each kinetic module computes a single tendency per variable per step. No linearization or Jacobian is required.
  • Vectorization. Every cell can be updated independently, which maps cleanly onto xarray and numpy array operations.
  • Interoperability. Operator splitting with the transport model is straightforward when both transport and kinetics use explicit schemes on the same time grid.

docs.title: Stability Considerations
docs.text:
Explicit Euler is conditionally stable. For a first-order decay process with rate \(k\), stability requires:

\[ \Delta t \leq \frac{2}{k} \]

For typical water quality rates (0.01 to 1 day\(^{-1}\)), this gives an upper bound of several hours to several days on \(\Delta t\). For the surface energy balance in TSM, the controlling time scale is the thermal response time of a shallow water column; a time step of one hour or less is typical.

Users who run into instability should first reduce the time step by a factor of two and rerun; if instability persists, inspect the parameter set for unphysically large rate constants.

docs.title: Positivity Clipping
docs.text:
Concentrations and temperatures are physical quantities with well-defined lower bounds. Explicit Euler can occasionally produce small negative values near zero (for example, when a depleting pool is pushed below zero by a large sink term). ClearWater applies a positivity clip after each update:

\[ C_{n+1} \leftarrow \max(C_{n+1}, C_{\min}) \]

where \(C_{\min}\) is either zero (for concentrations) or a small positive tolerance (for variables that appear in denominators). For water temperature, an upper bound is also applied.

Positivity clipping introduces a small mass non-conservation when activated, but for the magnitudes typically clipped (on the order of machine epsilon times the pool size) the effect on long-term mass balance is negligible. If clipping is invoked frequently on a variable, that is a signal that the time step is too large or that a parameter is driving the pool to zero too aggressively.

docs.title: Chunked Execution
docs.text:
Large simulations (high-resolution 2D grids times long time horizons) can easily produce state histories of tens to hundreds of gigabytes. ClearWater executes such simulations in chunks so that only a small portion of the state is in memory at any one time.

The chunking pattern follows the zarr chunk shape declared in the data backend (see Zarr Data Store). A typical pattern is:

flowchart LR
    A[Start of time chunk] --> B[Read state at t_n from zarr]
    B --> C[Compute kinetic tendencies for all cells]
    C --> D[Update state to t_n+1]
    D --> E[Write state at t_n+1 to zarr]
    E --> F{More steps in chunk?}
    F -- Yes --> B
    F -- No --> G[Flush chunk to disk, release memory]
    G --> H[Next time chunk]

Within a chunk, all cells are updated in a single vectorized array operation. Between chunks, the backend flushes completed time slices to disk and reclaims the memory. Peak memory scales with chunk size, not with total simulation size.

docs.title: Operator Splitting with Transport
docs.text:
ClearWater uses first-order operator splitting between transport and kinetics. Within each time step, the transport model advects and disperses the state fields first, then the ClearWater modules apply the cell-local kinetic tendencies. This is sometimes called sequential splitting.

For the rates typical of water quality modeling, operator splitting error is small compared to the uncertainty in kinetic parameters and is usually acceptable. Higher-order splitting schemes (Strang splitting) could be substituted if greater accuracy were required, but the current implementation has found first-order splitting sufficient across all validated applications.

docs.title: Reproducibility
docs.text: Because ClearWater uses deterministic vectorized array operations, two runs with the same initial conditions, parameters, and forcing produce bit-identical results on the same hardware. This makes it straightforward to verify that a parameter change produced the intended effect and to diff output files during calibration.

docs.title: Temperature Theory
docs.text: The Temperature Simulation Module (TSM) applies conservation of energy to a well-mixed water column in each computational cell. This page presents the theoretical basis for the surface energy balance and the heat flux formulations used by TSM. For the specific equations and parameter settings implemented in the module, see the TSM Energy Balance page.

docs.title: Conservation of Energy
docs.text:
For a well-mixed water column of volume \(V\) and surface area \(A_s\), the first law of thermodynamics gives:

\[ \rho_w \, c_{p,w} \, V \, \frac{\partial T_w}{\partial t} = \sum_i q_i \, A_i \]

where the sum runs over all heat flux terms \(q_i\) (W m\(^{-2}\)) acting on the corresponding interfacial area \(A_i\). The density \(\rho_w\) and specific heat \(c_{p,w}\) of water are treated as constants because their variation over the range of natural water temperatures is small.

docs.title: Heat Flux Components
docs.text:
The total surface energy balance decomposes into five components at the air-water interface and one at the sediment-water interface:

\[ q_{\text{net}} = q_{sw} + q_{lw,in} - q_{lw,out} - q_{lat} - q_{sen} + \underbrace{q_{sed} \, (A_b / A_s)}_{\text{bed contribution}} \]

docs.title: Shortwave Radiation
docs.text: Incoming shortwave radiation is largely independent of water temperature and depends on solar geometry, atmospheric transmission, and cloud cover. A fraction \(\alpha_s\) (the surface albedo) is reflected; the remainder is absorbed in the water column. For a well-mixed column, all absorbed shortwave is treated as a surface heat flux.

docs.title: Longwave Radiation
docs.text: Both the atmosphere and the water surface radiate in the longwave band according to the Stefan-Boltzmann law, modified by an effective emissivity. The net longwave exchange is typically negative (net energy loss) at night and small but variable during the day. Cloud cover enhances downwelling longwave by reflecting water-emitted radiation back to the surface.

docs.title: Latent Heat (Evaporation)
docs.text: Evaporation removes latent heat from the water at a rate proportional to the vapor pressure deficit between the saturated air immediately above the water surface and the overlying atmosphere. The wind function \(f(U_w)\) encapsulates the turbulent transfer efficiency. Evaporation is usually the dominant cooling term in summer.

docs.title: Sensible Heat
docs.text: Sensible heat transfer is driven by the air-water temperature difference and shares the same wind function as evaporation (Bowen ratio analogy). Sensible heat can go in either direction; the water often loses sensible heat at night and gains it on cold-air days.

docs.title: Sediment Heat Flux
docs.text: Heat conducts across the sediment-water interface according to Fourier's law, driven by the temperature gradient between the water and the underlying bed. Sediment heat flux is usually small compared to surface fluxes in deep water but can be significant in shallow streams, where the bed acts as a thermal reservoir that moderates diel temperature swings.

docs.title: Sign Convention
docs.text: All fluxes are written so that positive values add energy to the water column. Loss terms (outgoing longwave, latent, sensible when \(T_w > T_a\)) appear with negative signs in the governing equation.

docs.title: Physical Assumptions
docs.text:
The TSM energy balance rests on the following standard assumptions:

  • The water column is well mixed vertically within each cell (no stratification).
  • Density and specific heat of water are constant over the simulated range.
  • Shortwave radiation is absorbed uniformly in the water column.
  • The surface is a free water surface; ice cover and under-ice processes are not represented explicitly.
  • Heat storage in the sediment is represented by a single active layer with prescribed thickness and temperature.

For stratified reservoirs, ice-covered waters, or systems where vertical temperature structure matters, a more detailed model (for example, CE-QUAL-W2) should be used upstream of ClearWater.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text: See the TSM Energy Balance page for the exact flux equations as implemented, and the TSM Configuration page for the parameters required to evaluate them.

docs.title: User Guide
docs.text: The User Guide documents each component of the ClearWater water quality modeling framework. It covers the transport engine, the water quality kinetics modules, and the shared data layer, along with the configuration, inputs, and parameters that users provide to run a simulation.

docs.title: In This Section
docs.text:
• ClearWater-Riverine -- the two-dimensional, depth-averaged transport framework that reads HEC-RAS (Hydrologic Engineering Center's River Analysis System) 2D hydrodynamic output and solves the advection-diffusion equation for one or more constituents.
  • Temperature Simulation Module (TSM) -- computes water temperature through a surface energy balance, with heat exchange terms for solar radiation, longwave radiation, sensible and latent heat, and sediment-water heat flux.
  • General Constituents Simulation Module (GSM) -- simulates arbitrary constituents that follow first-order decay and optional settling, suitable for tracers, total dissolved solids, and user-defined substances that do not require specialized kinetics.
  • Nutrient Simulation Module v1 (NSM1) -- simulates the coupled cycling of nitrogen, phosphorus, carbon, dissolved oxygen, algae, pathogens, alkalinity, particulate organic matter, and carbonaceous biochemical oxygen demand (CBOD).
  • ClearWater-Data -- the shared data-access layer used by the transport engine and the kinetics modules, built on xarray with support for both in-memory and chunked zarr workflows.

docs.title: How the Components Fit Together
docs.text:
ClearWater-Riverine drives constituent transport across the mesh. At each time step, the transport engine calls into one or more kinetics modules (TSM, GSM, NSM1) to compute source and sink terms, which are then applied to the advected state variables. ClearWater-Data provides the VariableRegistry that all components share for state variable storage, lookup, and time indexing.

A typical coupled simulation combines ClearWater-Riverine with TSM (to compute temperature) and NSM1 (to compute nutrient and algal kinetics driven by that temperature). The Getting Started section walks through a minimal coupled run, and the Examples section provides end-to-end Jupyter notebooks for the Ohio River and other reference cases.

docs.title: Related Sections
docs.text:
• Getting Started -- installation, environment setup, and a minimal coupled simulation.
  • Theory -- the mathematical and physical formulations that underlie transport, heat exchange, and kinetic reactions.
  • API Reference -- auto-generated reference documentation for the Python classes and functions.
  • Developer Guide -- architecture, contribution guidelines, and the Process-based interface for adding a new kinetics module.

docs.title: ClearWater-Data
docs.text: ClearWater-Data is the shared data-access layer used by the ClearWater water quality and temperature modules. It provides a single interface for reading, writing, and indexing the state variables and static parameters that flow between the transport model and each kinetics module.

docs.title: In This Section
docs.text:
• Overview describes the role of ClearWater-Data and the xarray-based architecture that supports both in-memory and chunked (zarr) workflows.
  • Variable Registry documents the VariableRegistry application programming interface (API) for registering, looking up, and accessing state variables at specific time steps.
  • Zarr Data Store documents the ChunkedZarrDataStore for simulations that exceed memory or benefit from persistent, chunked input/output (I/O).

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: ClearWater-Data is the shared data-access layer used across the ClearWater water quality framework. It decouples the kinetic modules (TSM, NSM1, GSM, CSM, and MSM) from the storage backend so that the same module code runs against in-memory arrays, on-disk zarr stores, or spatially distributed fields supplied by a transport model. ClearWater-Data is built on xarray and numpy, which provide labeled multidimensional arrays with named dimensions for time, space, and variable.

docs.title: Design Goals
docs.text:
ClearWater-Data is designed to meet three requirements that recur across ClearWater simulations:

  • Uniform access. Every module reads and writes state variables through the same API, regardless of how the data are physically stored. This eliminates ad hoc per-module data plumbing.
  • Scale flexibility. Small simulations run entirely in memory with minimal overhead. Large simulations (long time series, high-resolution 2D grids, ensembles) can stream through a chunked zarr store without exhausting RAM.
  • Time-indexed history. Each state variable has an explicit time axis. Modules can request the value at the current time step, the previous time step, or any prior time, enabling multi-step integrators, diagnostics, and restart workflows.

docs.title: Core Components
docs.text:
Component Role VariableRegistry Central catalog of registered variables. Supports register, get_at_time, and set_at_time operations with dimension and type metadata. ChunkedZarrDataStore Disk-backed store that persists variables as chunked zarr arrays. Supports random access to time slices without loading the full history. In-memory backend Default backend that holds variables as xarray.DataArray objects in RAM. Used for short simulations and test fixtures.

Modules do not interact with the storage backend directly. They receive a registry, request variables by name, and write back updated values. The registry dispatches the underlying reads and writes to whichever backend is active.

docs.title: Variable Types
docs.text:
ClearWater-Data distinguishes three variable types that correspond to different update frequencies:

  • State variables are prognostic quantities integrated in time (for example, water temperature, NH4, DOX). They have a time dimension and are written at every step.
  • Dynamic variables are diagnostic or forcing fields that may change over time but are not integrated (for example, air temperature, wind speed, transport fluxes). They also carry a time dimension.
  • Static variables are parameters and coefficients that do not change during a simulation (for example, wind function coefficients, stoichiometric ratios). They are stored without a time dimension.

docs.title: Typical Workflow
docs.text:
A simulation using ClearWater-Data follows this pattern:

  1. Create a registry and choose a backend (in-memory or zarr).
  2. Register each state, dynamic, and static variable with its shape, dtype, and units.
  3. Initialize state variables at t = 0 using set_at_time.
  4. At each time step, the transport model and each kinetics module read and write variables through the registry.
  5. On completion, the registry is either discarded (in-memory) or closed to finalize the zarr store on disk.

docs.title: When to Use the Zarr Backend
docs.text:
The ChunkedZarrDataStore is the recommended backend when:

  • The simulation grid is large enough that holding the full history in memory is impractical.
  • Results must be persistent and accessible after the simulation completes.
  • Multiple processes or workflows need concurrent read access to the same simulation output.

For short tests, unit tests, or single-cell simulations, the in-memory backend is simpler and faster.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
• See Variable Registry for the API used to register and access variables.
  • See Zarr Data Store for chunking strategy, memory footprint, and disk layout.

docs.title: Variable Registry
docs.text: The VariableRegistry is the central catalog that ClearWater modules use to read and write state, dynamic, and static variables. It provides a consistent API regardless of whether the underlying storage is an in-memory xarray.Dataset or a chunked zarr store on disk.

docs.title: Variable Types
docs.text:
The registry supports three variable types that correspond to different update behaviors.

Type Time Axis Mutable During Simulation Typical Examples State Yes Yes (integrated each step) T_water, NH4, DOX, Ap Dynamic Yes Yes (read from forcing or transport) T_air, U_wind, q_sw_inc Static No No Stoichiometric ratios, wind function coefficients, half-saturation constants

docs.title: Registering Variables
docs.text:
Each variable must be declared before it can be read or written. Registration fixes the variable's type, dimensions, data type, and units.

from clearwater_data import VariableRegistry

registry = VariableRegistry()

registry.register(
    name="T_water",
    kind="state",
    dims=("time", "cell"),
    dtype="float64",
    units="degC",
)

registry.register(
    name="k_20_NH4",
    kind="static",
    dims=("cell",),
    dtype="float64",
    units="1/day",
)

docs.title: Reading Variables at a Time Step
docs.text:
Use get_at_time to retrieve the value of a state or dynamic variable at a specific time index. Static variables are retrieved with get.

T_now = registry.get_at_time("T_water", t=step)
T_prev = registry.get_at_time("T_water", t=step - 1)
k20 = registry.get("k_20_NH4")

get_at_time returns an xarray.DataArray aligned to the spatial dimensions of the variable. The returned array may be a lazy dask-backed view when the zarr backend is active.

docs.title: Writing Variables at a Time Step
docs.text:
Use set_at_time to write a state or dynamic variable at a specific time index. The value being written must match the registered dimensions and dtype.

registry.set_at_time("T_water", t=step + 1, value=T_new)

Static variables are written once during initialization with set.

docs.title: Dimension and Type Checking
docs.text: The registry validates dimensions and dtypes on every read and write. Attempts to write a variable with mismatched shape or incompatible dtype raise an error before any data are stored. This catches shape bugs and unit errors early.

docs.title: Backend Selection
docs.text:
The registry dispatches reads and writes to whichever backend is active. To switch between in-memory and zarr storage, construct the registry with the appropriate backend:

# In-memory backend (default)
registry = VariableRegistry()

# Zarr-backed registry
from clearwater_data import ChunkedZarrDataStore
store = ChunkedZarrDataStore(path="./sim_output.zarr", chunks={"time": 24, "cell": 1000})
registry = VariableRegistry(backend=store)

See Zarr Data Store for details on chunking and disk layout.

docs.title: Typical Usage in a Time Step Loop
docs.text:
for step in range(n_steps):
    T_now = registry.get_at_time("T_water", t=step)
    T_air = registry.get_at_time("T_air", t=step)
    U = registry.get_at_time("U_wind", t=step)

    T_new = tsm_step(T_now, T_air, U, registry.get("a_wind"), ...)

    registry.set_at_time("T_water", t=step + 1, value=T_new)

docs.title: Summary of API
docs.text: Method Purpose register(name, kind, dims, dtype, units) Declare a new variable get(name) Retrieve a static variable set(name, value) Write a static variable get_at_time(name, t) Retrieve a state or dynamic variable at time index t set_at_time(name, t, value) Write a state or dynamic variable at time index t variables() List all registered variable names close() Flush and close the underlying backend (no-op for in-memory)

docs.title: Chunked Zarr Data Store
docs.text: The ChunkedZarrDataStore is the disk-backed storage backend for ClearWater-Data. It persists every registered variable as a chunked zarr array, which allows ClearWater to run simulations whose full state history does not fit in memory and to produce output that is readable by any tool in the xarray / zarr ecosystem.

docs.title: When to Use the Zarr Backend
docs.text:
Choose the zarr backend when one or more of the following conditions hold:

  • The simulation grid times the number of time steps exceeds available RAM.
  • Output must persist on disk for post-processing, visualization, or restart.
  • Multiple downstream tools (Jupyter notebooks, Dask workflows, external viewers) need random-access reads of the output.
  • Simulations run long enough that intermediate crashes would otherwise lose all results.

For short simulations, unit tests, or single-cell scenarios, the default in-memory backend is simpler.

docs.title: Storage Layout
docs.text:
Each registered variable becomes a zarr array under the store's root directory. The array dimensions match the variable's registered dimensions. Attributes such as units and long names are preserved in the zarr metadata.

A typical on-disk layout for a 2D simulation with state variables T_water and NH4 and forcing variable T_air looks like:

sim_output.zarr/
    T_water/
        .zarray
        .zattrs
        0.0, 0.1, ... (chunk files)
    NH4/
        ...
    T_air/
        ...
    .zgroup
    .zattrs

docs.title: Chunking Strategy
docs.text:
Chunks are the fundamental unit of I/O in zarr. Choosing chunk sizes well is the single most important tuning decision for the zarr backend.

General guidelines:

  • Align chunks with access patterns. ClearWater modules read and write one time slice per step across all cells. A chunk shape such as {"time": 24, "cell": N_cells} (one-day time chunks across the whole grid) works well when access is time-step-sequential.
  • Target 1--100 MB per chunk. Very small chunks generate excessive metadata overhead; very large chunks force loading more than needed.
  • Match chunk boundaries to analysis needs. If downstream analysis aggregates by day or by region, align the chunk boundaries so aggregations touch the minimum number of chunks.

Specify chunks when constructing the store:

from clearwater_data import ChunkedZarrDataStore

store = ChunkedZarrDataStore(
    path="./sim_output.zarr",
    chunks={"time": 24, "cell": 10000},
)

docs.title: Memory Footprint
docs.text:
The zarr backend holds only the active chunks in memory. When a module requests a time slice, the store loads the chunk containing that slice, returns a view, and releases the chunk when it is no longer referenced. Peak memory usage is therefore approximately:

\[ \text{Peak RAM} \approx \sum_{\text{variables}} \text{(chunk size)} \times \text{(active chunks per variable)} \]

For a grid of 100,000 cells, 8-byte floats, and a chunk shape of {"time": 24, "cell": 10000}, each chunk is \(24 \times 10{,}000 \times 8 = 1.9\) MB. A registry with 15 state variables touches roughly 30 MB when a single time slice is active, independent of the total number of time steps.

docs.title: Opening, Appending, and Reading
docs.text:
Create a new store by passing a path that does not yet exist. Re-open an existing store by passing the same path; the store detects the existing zarr group and attaches to it. Reads can proceed from any tool that understands zarr:

import xarray as xr

ds = xr.open_zarr("./sim_output.zarr")
print(ds)
T = ds["T_water"].sel(time=slice("2024-01-01", "2024-01-31"))

docs.title: Closing the Store
docs.text: Call store.close() (or registry.close() if you are working through the registry) when the simulation completes. This flushes any pending writes and finalizes the zarr metadata. Most zarr operations are write-through, so data loss from an unexpected crash is typically limited to the currently buffered chunk.

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
• Write one full time slice per step rather than many small per-cell writes. The chunking strategy assumes contiguous spatial writes.
  • If the simulation is embarrassingly parallel across cells, ensure that parallel workers write to disjoint chunk regions to avoid contention.
  • For long simulations, periodically verify disk usage; zarr produces one small file per chunk, and file-system inode limits can become the binding constraint before disk space does.

docs.title: Related Pages
docs.text:
• Variable Registry for the API used to read and write variables.
  • Overview for the broader architecture of ClearWater-Data.

docs.title: General Constituents Simulation Module (GSM)
docs.text: The General Constituents Simulation Module (GSM) simulates arbitrary water quality constituents that follow first-order decay and optional settling. GSM is intended for conservative tracers, total dissolved solids, total suspended solids, simple organic compounds, and any user-defined constituent that does not require the specialized kinetics of NSM1, CSM, or MSM.

docs.title: In This Section
docs.text:
• Overview describes the GSM kinetic formulation and common use cases.
  • Configuration lists the parameters required to define one or more generic constituents.

docs.title: When to Use GSM
docs.text: Use GSM when a constituent can be adequately represented by first-order decay, temperature correction, and constant settling velocity. For nutrients, use NSM1. For contaminants with sorption and phase partitioning, use CSM. For mercury speciation, use MSM.

docs.title: GSM Configuration
docs.text: You configure GSM as a list of constituents. Each constituent has its own kinetic parameters and initial condition. The module supports an arbitrary number of constituents, and GSM integrates them independently at each time step.

docs.title: Per-Constituent Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Units Description name string Constituent name used for output labeling units string Concentration units (for example, mg/L, ug/L, CFU/100mL) k_20 day\(^{-1}\) First-order decay rate at 20 degrees C. Set to 0 for a conservative constituent. theta dimensionless Arrhenius temperature coefficient. Typical values are 1.0 (no temperature dependence) to 1.08. v_s m day\(^{-1}\) Settling velocity. Set to 0 for a dissolved constituent. C0 same as units Initial concentration

docs.title: Temperature Correction
docs.text:
GSM applies the standard Arrhenius correction to the decay rate:

\[ k(T) = k_{20} \, \theta^{T - 20} \]

where \(T\) is the water temperature in degrees C at the current cell and time step. See the Kinetics theory page for background on the Arrhenius formulation.

docs.title: Settling
docs.text: GSM applies the settling flux as a loss term proportional to \(v_s / H\), where \(H\) is the cell water depth supplied by the transport model. The settled mass leaves the water column, and GSM does not track it further. If resuspension or sediment-water coupling is required, use NSM1 or a specialized module.

docs.title: Example Configuration
docs.text:
The following example configures three constituents: a conservative tracer, total suspended solids with settling, and a temperature-dependent decaying organic compound.

gsm:
  constituents:
    - name: Tracer
      units: mg/L
      k_20: 0.0
      theta: 1.0
      v_s: 0.0
      C0: 1.0

    - name: TSS
      units: mg/L
      k_20: 0.0
      theta: 1.0
      v_s: 0.5
      C0: 50.0

    - name: Generic_Organic
      units: mg/L
      k_20: 0.1
      theta: 1.047
      v_s: 0.0
      C0: 10.0

docs.title: Initial Conditions
docs.text: You may supply initial concentrations as a scalar (applied uniformly across the grid) or as a spatial field matching the transport model grid.

docs.title: Boundary Conditions
docs.text: You must supply boundary inflows for each GSM constituent through the transport model. GSM does not impose boundary fluxes directly; GSM acts only on the cell-local state provided by the host model.

docs.title: Calibration Guidance
docs.text:
• For conservative tracers, verify that simulated concentrations match transport-only behavior before enabling decay or settling.
  • For first-order decay constituents, estimate \(k_{20}\) and \(\theta\) from laboratory incubations, literature values, or field calibration against observed concentrations.
  • For settling particulate constituents, \(v_s\) depends strongly on particle size distribution and flocculation behavior. Calibrate against observed deposition patterns or suspended sediment concentrations.

docs.title: Related Modules
docs.text:
• NSM1 for coupled nutrient and algae biogeochemistry.
  • See the Kinetics theory page for the general decay and temperature correction formulations used throughout ClearWater.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: The General Constituents Simulation Module (GSM) provides a lightweight kinetic framework for any number of user-defined water quality constituents. GSM integrates each constituent independently using a first-order decay law with Arrhenius temperature correction and an optional settling flux. GSM is designed for substances that do not warrant the specialized biogeochemistry of the nutrient, contaminant, or mercury modules.

docs.title: What GSM Simulates
docs.text:
For each constituent \(C\), GSM integrates the cell-local budget:

\[ \frac{\partial C}{\partial t} = -k(T) \, C - \frac{v_s}{H} \, C \]

where:

  • \(C\) is the constituent concentration (user-defined units, for example mg L\(^{-1}\)).
  • \(k(T) = k_{20} \, \theta^{T-20}\) is the first-order decay rate at the current water temperature \(T\) (day\(^{-1}\)).
  • \(k_{20}\) is the decay rate at 20 degrees C.
  • \(\theta\) is the Arrhenius temperature coefficient.
  • \(v_s\) is the settling velocity (m day\(^{-1}\)).
  • \(H\) is the water column depth (m).

Setting \(k_{20} = 0\) and \(v_s = 0\) produces a fully conservative tracer. Setting only \(v_s = 0\) produces a dissolved reactive constituent. Setting only \(k_{20} = 0\) produces a settling particulate tracer.

docs.title: Typical Use Cases
docs.text: Constituent Type Decay Rate Settling Velocity Notes Conservative tracer (salinity, chloride, dye) 0 0 Advection and dispersion only; checks transport behavior Total suspended solids 0 > 0 Particulate tracer with gravitational settling Generic organic compound > 0 0 First-order biodegradation with temperature dependence Bacterial indicator > 0 0 Temperature-dependent die-off User-defined varies varies Any combination supported

docs.title: Module Scope
docs.text:
GSM computes only the cell-local kinetic tendencies. Advection, dispersion, and boundary fluxes are handled by the external transport model (for example, HEC-RAS 2D via ClearWater-Riverine). GSM receives the current concentration field and water temperature, computes the decay and settling tendencies, and returns the updated concentrations to the transport model.

GSM integrates each constituent independently and does not represent reactions between constituents. If coupling between species is required, use the appropriate specialized module or extend GSM with custom kinetics.

docs.title: Inputs at a Glance
docs.text: Category Examples Constituent properties Decay rate at 20 degrees C, Arrhenius coefficient, settling velocity Environmental drivers Water temperature, water depth Initial conditions Initial concentration for each constituent

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text: GSM produces an updated concentration field for each configured constituent at every time step. Decay and settling fluxes are available as diagnostic outputs for mass balance verification.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text: See the Configuration page for the full list of parameters and an example configuration for multiple constituents.

docs.title: Nutrient Simulation Module v1 (NSM1)
docs.text: The Nutrient Simulation Module v1 (NSM1) simulates the coupled cycling of nitrogen, phosphorus, carbon, dissolved oxygen, algae, pathogens, alkalinity, particulate organic matter, and carbonaceous biochemical oxygen demand (CBOD) in surface waters. NSM1 is the primary water quality kinetics engine of ClearWater.

docs.title: In This Section
docs.text:
• Overview describes the 13 state variables, their interactions, and the coupling structure that drives the module.
  • State-variable reference pages (floating algae, benthic algae, nitrogen, phosphorus, carbon, CBOD, dissolved oxygen, pathogens, alkalinity) document the rate equations, parameters, and default values for each group.

docs.title: Related Theory
docs.text: See the Kinetics page for the general formulations (Arrhenius correction, Monod limitation, stoichiometric ratios) used throughout NSM1.

docs.title: Alkalinity (Alk)
docs.text:
Alkalinity is the acid-neutralizing capacity of water, operationally defined as the sum of titratable bases. In surface waters dominated by the carbonate system, alkalinity is well approximated by:

\[ Alk \approx [HCO_3^-] + 2[CO_3^{2-}] + [OH^-] - [H^+] \]

NSM1 tracks total alkalinity Alk as a prognostic state variable in units of mg-CaCO3 L-1. Alkalinity determines the pH buffering capacity of the water column, sets the equilibrium distribution of dissolved inorganic carbon among CO2, bicarbonate, and carbonate species, and controls the saturation state of calcium carbonate minerals. Biological processes that produce or consume hydrogen ions (H+) shift alkalinity, and NSM1 accounts for the dominant biological drivers explicitly.

docs.title: Role in Water Quality
docs.text:
Alkalinity in NSM1 is driven entirely by biologically mediated transformations of nitrogen and by autotrophic growth and respiration. The model includes six flux terms:

  • Nitrification of NH4 to NO3 releases H+ and decreases alkalinity.
  • Denitrification of NO3 to N2 consumes H+ and increases alkalinity.
  • Algal growth on NH4 consumes H+ and increases alkalinity; algal growth on NO3 releases H+ and decreases alkalinity.
  • Algal respiration releases NH4, consuming H+ and increasing alkalinity.
  • Benthic algal growth and respiration contribute the same way, scaled by the benthic coverage fraction and depth.

NSM1 does not explicitly simulate CO\(_2\) reaeration effects on alkalinity (CO\(_2\) exchange affects DIC but is alkalinity-neutral) or mineral dissolution and precipitation.

docs.title: Governing Equation
docs.text:
The Alk mass balance, implemented in dAlkdt at processes.py ~line 3413, combines the six biologically driven terms:

\[ \frac{d[Alk]}{dt} = F_{denit} - F_{nit} - F_{ApG} + F_{ApR} - F_{AbG} + F_{AbR} \]

Each flux is expressed in mg-CaCO3 L-1 d-1. The factor 50000 (equivalent weight of CaCO3 in mg eq-1) appears in every term to convert from molar equivalents to mg-CaCO3.

docs.title: Alkalinity change from nitrification
docs.text:
Nitrification of 1 mole of NH4 releases 2 moles of H+, decreasing alkalinity. The Alk_nitrification routine at ~line 3284 computes:

\[ F_{nit} = r_{alkn} \left(1 - e^{-KNR \cdot DOX}\right) k_{nit}(T) \cdot NH4 \cdot 50000 \]

The DOX inhibition term \((1 - e^{-KNR \cdot DOX})\) matches the oxygen dependence of the nitrification rate in the nitrogen and DOX modules. When use_DOX is false, NSM1 drops the inhibition factor.

docs.title: Alkalinity change from denitrification
docs.text:
Denitrification of NO3 to N2 consumes H+, increasing alkalinity. The Alk_denitrification routine at ~line 3246 computes:

\[ F_{denit} = r_{alkden} \left(1 - \frac{DOX}{DOX + K_{sOxdn}}\right) k_{dnit}(T) \cdot NO3 \cdot 50000 \]

The DOX inhibition term promotes denitrification only at low oxygen. When use_DOX is false, the oxygen term drops out.

docs.title: Alkalinity change from algal growth
docs.text:
Algal growth on ammonium consumes H+ (increases alkalinity); growth on nitrate releases H+ (decreases alkalinity). The Alk_algal_growth routine at ~line 3322 computes the net effect weighted by the ammonium preference fraction \(f_{NH4}^{Ap}\):

\[ F_{ApG} = \left[ r_{alkaa} \, f_{NH4}^{Ap} - r_{alkan} \, (1 - f_{NH4}^{Ap}) \right] \cdot ApGrowth \cdot r_{ca} \cdot 50000 \]

The sign convention in the governing equation subtracts \(F_{ApG}\), reflecting that growth on NO3 is the net alkalinity-consuming pathway when the ammonium fraction is low.

docs.title: Alkalinity change from algal respiration
docs.text:
Algal respiration returns NH4 to the water, which consumes H+ and increases alkalinity. The Alk_algal_respiration routine at ~line 3345 computes:

\[ F_{ApR} = ApResp \cdot r_{alkaa} \cdot r_{ca} \cdot 50000 \]

docs.title: Alkalinity change from benthic algae
docs.text:
Benthic algal growth and respiration follow the same stoichiometry as floating algae, with the benthic ratios r_alkba and r_alkbn, the benthic C-to-dry-weight ratio rcb, and additional scaling by the benthic coverage fraction Fb and inverse depth \(1/h\). The Alk_benthic_algae_growth (~line 3364) and Alk_benthic_algae_respiration (~line 3391) routines compute:

\[ F_{AbG} = \frac{F_b}{h} \left[ r_{alkba} \, f_{NH4}^{Ab} - r_{alkbn} \, (1 - f_{NH4}^{Ab}) \right] \cdot AbGrowth \cdot r_{cb} \cdot 50000 \] \[ F_{AbR} = \frac{F_b}{h} \cdot r_{alkba} \cdot AbResp \cdot r_{cb} \cdot 50000 \]

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Units Scope Description Default r_alkaa eq / ug-Chla alkalinity Alkalinity change per unit algal growth when NH4 is the N source 14/106/12/1000 r_alkan eq / ug-Chla alkalinity Alkalinity change per unit algal growth when NO3 is the N source 18/106/12/1000 r_alkn eq / mg-N alkalinity Alkalinity change per unit NH4 nitrified 2/14/1000 r_alkden eq / mg-N alkalinity Alkalinity change per unit NO3 denitrified 4/14/1000 r_alkba eq / mg-D alkalinity Alkalinity change per unit benthic algal growth when NH4 is the N source 14/106/12/1000 r_alkbn eq / mg-D alkalinity Alkalinity change per unit benthic algal growth when NO3 is the N source 18/106/12/1000 KNR mg-O2 L-1 nitrogen Oxygen inhibition factor for nitrification 0.6 KsOxdn mg-O2 L-1 nitrogen Half-saturation oxygen inhibition for denitrification 0.1 { .parameter-table }

The Redfield-derived ratios (14/106/12/1000 and 18/106/12/1000) encode the number of moles of H+ produced or consumed per mole of algal C fixed through the Redfield stoichiometry (C106 H263 O110 N16 P), divided by the C:Chl conversion and unit factors. Each ratio is multiplied by 50000 mg-CaCO3 eq-1 inside the flux functions to produce mg-CaCO3 L-1 d-1.

docs.title: Couplings with Other State Variables
docs.text:
Alkalinity is a passive tracer in NSM1: it is affected by other state variables but does not feed back into them. Its couplings are:

  • Ammonia (NH4) drives nitrification loss of alkalinity and, through algal uptake, controls the sign of the algal growth term.
  • Nitrate (NO3) drives denitrification gain of alkalinity and contributes to the algal growth term when algae use NO3.
  • Floating algae (Ap) drives \(F_{ApG}\) and \(F_{ApR}\).
  • Benthic algae (Ab) drives \(F_{AbG}\) and \(F_{AbR}\).
  • Dissolved oxygen (DOX) modulates the nitrification and denitrification rates through their oxygen dependence.
  • Depth (h) scales the benthic algae contributions.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
global_parameters:
  use_Alk: true
  use_NH4: true
  use_NO3: true
  use_DOX: true
  use_Algae: true
  use_Balgae: true

alkalinity_parameters:
  r_alkaa: 1.100629e-05   # 14 / 106 / 12 / 1000
  r_alkan: 1.415094e-05   # 18 / 106 / 12 / 1000
  r_alkn: 1.428571e-04    # 2 / 14 / 1000
  r_alkden: 2.857143e-04  # 4 / 14 / 1000
  r_alkba: 1.100629e-05
  r_alkbn: 1.415094e-05

Unit conventions

The alkalinity stoichiometric ratios are stored as pure equivalence ratios (mol eq per unit biomass or nitrogen). Each flux function multiplies by 50000 (the equivalent weight of CaCO3 in mg per mol eq) to produce the final flux in mg-CaCO3 L-1 d-1. Do not pre-multiply the ratios by 50000 in the configuration file.

docs.title: Implementation Notes
docs.text:
• The alkalinity process is implemented in src/clearwater_modules/processes/alkalinity.py as the Alkalinity Process subclass. The rate method sums six contributions: denitrification, nitrification, algal_growth, algal_respiration, benthic_algae_growth, and benthic_algae_respiration. The r_alkn stoichiometric ratio is applied uniformly in every branch of the nitrification term, with or without the DOX inhibition factor.
  • Default constants: DEFAULT_ALKALINITY in src/clearwater_modules/processes/constants.py.
